name: Grade 12
theme: Vocation, faith in the world and the last things

units.title: Discerning your vocation
units.eq: What does God ask of me?

lessons.title: Every person is called
lessons.idea: God calls every person to holiness and to a particular way of life. Vocation begins with Baptism and unfolds through discernment: prayer, the sacraments, the Church’s guidance and honest self-knowledge. Jeremiah’s call shows that God knows and chooses us before we do.
lessons.question: How do I discern?
lessons.activity: “Vocation journal” (40 min). Students start a four-part journal: gifts (what I do well), joys (what gives me life), needs (what the world needs that I notice) and invitations (moments I sensed a call). They write a first entry on each and name one trusted person to discuss it with.
teach: All are called to holiness (CCC 825, 2013; Lumen Gentium 40). Each also has a particular vocation within the one mission of the Church (CCC 1877–1879, 897–933).
God’s call is personal: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). It comes through gifts, circumstances, desires purified by prayer and the Church’s discernment.
Discernment uses Ignatian tools: notice consolations and desolations, pray with Scripture, seek spiritual direction, test in action (CCC 2690).
Reassure students: God does not hide his will; a vocation is a gift to be received, not a puzzle to solve alone.
quiz: Which statement best separates the universal call from a particular vocation?|Only priests and religious have a vocation|Everyone is called to holiness; a vocation is the particular way a person lives it|A vocation is a career choice made once at 18|The universal call applies only to the baptized who are confirmed|1|CCC 825, 2013 and CCC 1877–1879: holiness is for all; each lives it in a state of life.

In Ignatian discernment, “desolation” is best described as…|Any sadness, which proves a choice is wrong|The end of prayer|A sign that God is angry|A movement toward discouragement and away from faith, hope and love|3|It is a movement away from God; it must be read with care and counsel, not by mood alone.

Jeremiah 1:5 (“before I formed you…I knew you”) is used in this lesson to show that…|God’s call precedes our choosing and invites a free response|God’s plan is a secret code to be cracked|Doubt disqualifies a person|Vocations are fixed by birth order|0|God takes the initiative; we respond freely (CCC 2232).
lessons.saint: Peter Faber: a shepherd boy from the Alps, the first priest of the Jesuits, who changed people by listening.
misc: “A vocation means the priesthood or religious life.”
“If I choose wrong, I have ruined God’s plan.”
lessons.mem: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you.” (Jeremiah 1:5)
lessons.hook: Read Jeremiah 1:4–8 aloud. Ask: “What excuse does Jeremiah give? What does God answer?” Students name excuses they use when something feels too big.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the difference between the universal call to holiness and a particular vocation, and name one step in discernment.

script.open: Hand out index cards. Ask each person to write, anonymously, the one question about their future that they think about most. Collect, shuffle and read a few aloud. Say, “These are all vocation questions.”
teach: Say: “The word vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call. The Church teaches that every person is called by God. The first call is universal: to know, love and serve God, and to be holy. Vatican II’s Lumen Gentium chapter 5 is titled ‘The Universal Call to Holiness.’ All Christians, ‘of whatever state or rank,’ are called to the fullness of Christian life and perfection of charity. This call comes in Baptism. Then there is a personal call: God has a particular plan for each of us. ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you.’ (Jeremiah 1:5) The saints say that the one is the path to the other: by being faithful where we are, we find our particular call.”

Say: “How do we discern? Discernment is a skill of listening to God and acting wisely. Ignatius of Loyola taught that we notice interior movements: consolation (a deep, lasting peace and love of God that leads us to give ourselves) and desolation (restlessness, discouragement, being drawn away from God). We look at what is life-giving over time. We pray with Scripture. We examine our gifts, desires and the needs of the world. We seek counsel from wise people: parents, priests, mentors. We notice how God’s call often comes through ordinary things, desires and circumstances. And we make a choice and test it. God’s will is generally not a hidden secret to be uncovered like a code, but a path to be walked in freedom with prayer.”

Say: “Some common difficulties. Fear: ‘What if I choose wrong?’ God is more concerned with our fidelity than a perfect answer. Many paths can be holy. Pressure: from parents, peers or culture. We need freedom. Doubt: ‘Am I good enough?’ Moses, Jeremiah and Mary all asked. Impatience: God often reveals the call one step at a time. The question is often not ‘Which is the one right life?’ but ‘What is the next faithful step?’ Peter Faber was anxious and scrupulous; he learned to trust. He changed people by friendship and attention. And Matthew 11:28: ‘Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.’ A vocation is not a burden but a gift.”
ask: What does the word ‘vocation’ mean? (A call.)
What is the universal call? (To holiness, in Baptism.)
What are consolation and desolation? (Ignatius’s names for movements toward and away from God.)
practice: Draw three overlapping circles: what I’m good at, what I love, what the world needs.
Write three items in each.
Look for overlaps and note them in the center.
Choose one next step to test, such as a conversation, volunteering or a course, and write when you will do it.
script.close: Pray the Suscipe or: “Lord, show me your way and give me the courage to walk it.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Talk with someone you trust about your discernment.”

tryit: Write what you are good at, what the world needs and what you love.
Look for where they overlap.
Name one next step to test it.
lessons.saintStory:
Pierre Favre, or Peter Faber, was born in 1506 in a village in the Savoy Alps, to a poor family. As a boy, he kept the family’s sheep, and at about seven, he made a private vow of chastity. He was bright and was sent to study in Paris, where he shared a room at the Collège Sainte-Barbe with two others: the Basque soldier Ignatius of Loyola, and Francis Xavier, an ambitious young Navarrese.
Faber was shy and anxious about his scruples. Ignatius helped him with patience and the Spiritual Exercises, and Faber became his first companion. He was ordained a priest in 1534 and was the one who celebrated the Mass at Montmartre where the little group took their vows. They were the first Jesuits.
He preached and gave retreats across Germany, Spain and Portugal, at a time of religious division. His method was to begin with friendship and listening, not argument. He died in Rome in 1546, at forty. Pope Francis, a Jesuit, called him a model and added him to the canon of saints in 2013.

lessons.title: Marriage, priesthood, consecrated life, single life
lessons.idea: The Church recognizes four ways of living out the call to holiness: marriage, the ordained priesthood and diaconate, consecrated life, and single life lived for God. Each is a real vocation with its own graces and challenges, and each needs the others.
lessons.question: What are the criteria for discernment?
lessons.activity: “Interview someone in each vocation” (45 min). Over a week, students interview a married person, a priest or deacon, a consecrated religious and a committed single person. They ask: How did you know? What is the hardest part? What surprised you? Present findings in a one-page comparison.
teach: Marriage is a covenant and a path of holiness for the couple and children (CCC 1601–1666). Holy Orders configures a man to Christ the head and servant (CCC 1536–1600).

Consecrated life lives the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience as a sign of the Kingdom (CCC 914–933). Single life can be a gift of availability when chosen for God, and also a circumstance that is lived in faith.
None is “higher” in dignity; each is higher in what God asks of that person (CCC 1620). Vatican II teaches a universal call to holiness.
Pray for vocations. Discernment is communal as well as personal.
quiz: Which statement best reflects Church teaching on marriage and consecrated virginity?|Both are optional for Christians|Marriage is a lesser, merely natural state|Marriage is a sacrament and a real path to holiness, and the Church also esteems virginity for the Kingdom as a special sign of the life to come (CCC 1619–1620)|Only celibates are called to holiness|2|CCC 1619–1620 and CCC 2013: each state of life is a way of holiness; neither is outside the call.
The evangelical counsels are…|Poverty, chastity and obedience|Fasting, prayer and almsgiving|Prudence, justice and fortitude|Faith, hope and charity|0|CCC 915.

A single person who lives for others and prays faithfully is…|Excused from holiness|In a waiting room until marriage|Not part of the Church’s mission|Living a real vocation if it is a gift offered to God and neighbor|3|The call to holiness belongs to all; single life can be a vocation.
lessons.life: Talk with someone in a vocation.
lessons.saint: The family of Basil the Great: married parents, a consecrated sister, a priest and two bishops, all honored as saints.
misc: “Marriage is the default; priesthood and religious life are rare exceptions.”
lessons.mem: “Each has his own special gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.” (1 Corinthians 7:7)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Corinthians 7:7: “Each has his own gift from God.” Ask: “Why would Paul say that both marriage and celibacy are gifts?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe each of the four states of life and what each witnesses to.

script.open: Write on the board: Marriage, Priesthood, Consecrated life, Single life. Ask, “Which of these do you think is the ‘best’ vocation? Which is the ‘easiest’? Which is the one you know least about?” Take honest answers.
teach: Say: “The Church has traditionally spoken of four states of life. Marriage: a man and a woman who give themselves to each other for life, open to children. It is a sacrament, a path of holiness through love, sacrifice, forgiveness and raising a family. Holy Orders: men called to serve as deacons, priests or bishops, to teach, sanctify and lead the Church. In the Latin Church, priests are celibate. Consecrated life: those who profess the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience: monks, nuns, friars, sisters, consecrated virgins, hermits, members of secular institutes. They are a sign of the Kingdom and give their lives to prayer and service. Single life: those who remain unmarried, for various reasons, and live their baptismal vocation in service. Some make private commitments.”

Say: “None is superior in dignity, though the Church teaches that consecrated virginity for the Kingdom is objectively a higher calling than marriage (Trent; Familiaris Consortio 16) in the sense that it anticipates the life of heaven, where ‘they neither marry nor are given in marriage.’ But for each person, the best vocation is the one God calls them to. Paul wrote: ‘Each has his own special gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.’ (1 Corinthians 7:7) Marriage and celibacy are not rivals. They need each other: families nurture vocations, and celibates remind married people of the Kingdom. Both are forms of love. The Church needs all.”

Say: “What does each demand? Marriage asks fidelity, patience, forgiveness, openness to life, daily sacrifice. Priesthood asks availability, celibacy, obedience to the bishop, sacrifice of one’s own plans. Consecrated life asks radical detachment, community and obedience. Single life asks discipline to avoid isolation, and intentional community and service. All ask prayer and sacramental life. And all are, in different ways, a gift of self: love. The Church’s teaching is that the vocation must be chosen freely; no one should be pushed. Discerning a vocation typically takes time: a period of dating or a period of seminary or religious formation. If you are drawn to priesthood or religious life, contact a vocation director. If you’re drawn to marriage, prepare by growing in virtue and choosing well.”
ask: What are the four states of life? (Marriage, Holy Orders, consecrated life, single life.)
Is any state a better path to holiness for everyone? (No; the best is the one God calls you to.)
How does celibacy relate to marriage? (They complement each other.)
practice: Make a four-column chart: Marriage / Priesthood / Consecrated life / Single life.
In each, write a saint, what it asks, what it gives the Church, and one question you have.
Underline which attracts you and which frightens you.
Share one honest reaction with a partner.
script.close: Pray for vocations of every kind: “Lord, give us holy families, priests, religious and single people who serve you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a married person, a priest or sister, and a single adult how they knew.”

tryit: Describe the four paths and what each gives to the Church.
Name a saint for each.
Write what attracts and what frightens you about each.
lessons.saintStory:
In Cappadocia, in what is now Turkey, in the fourth century, a remarkable family produced a number of saints. Basil the Elder, a lawyer and teacher, and Emmelia were married and raised ten children. They had lost property in a persecution and kept their faith. Emmelia’s mother, Macrina the Elder, had lived through the persecution of Diocletian and taught her grandchildren the faith.
Their eldest daughter, Macrina, chose to be consecrated to God, and turned the family estate into a community for prayer and service. One son, Basil, became bishop of Caesarea, a great theologian and founder of monasteries. Another, Gregory, was married and later became bishop of Nyssa. Another, Peter, was a monk and then bishop of Sebaste. Naucratius, who died young, lived as a hermit and cared for the poor.
So from one household came a married couple, a consecrated woman, a hermit, a monk, and bishops. Together they show the variety of vocations in one family, all working toward one thing: holiness.

lessons.title: Work and gifts
lessons.idea: Work is part of God’s plan: humans share in his creative work and sanctify the world by it. A vocation includes how we use our gifts for others. Work has dignity, and workers have rights.
lessons.question: How can work be holy?
lessons.activity: “Reflect on a career” (40 min). Students write about a career or field they are considering, answering: How could this serve others? What would it ask of me morally? What could go wrong? Where could I be a Christian witness? Pair up and share.
teach: Work is a duty and a way to participate in God’s creative work (CCC 2427). Laborem Exercens (John Paul II): work is “for man,” not man for work.
Rights of workers: just wage, safe conditions, rest, the right to organize (CCC 2433–2436). Employers have duties of justice (CCC 2434).
Rest is part of God’s plan: Sabbath (CCC 2184–2188). Work must not become an idol.
Vocation includes how we love in daily work: “Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord” (Colossians 3:23). St Joseph the Worker is a model.
quiz: In Catholic teaching, the primary reason work has dignity is that…|It earns money|The worker is a person made in God’s image, and work shares in God’s creative action|It keeps people busy|The state requires it|1|CCC 2426–2428; Laborem Exercens.
Which of these is a right of workers named in the Catechism?|A guaranteed promotion|A ban on all employers|A just wage and the freedom to organize|Exemption from all risk|2|CCC 2434–2435.

Why does the Church insist on rest (Sabbath) alongside work?|Because people are more than their productivity, and rest orders life toward God and others|Because work is evil|Because rest earns salvation|Because laws forbid factories|0|CCC 2184–2188.
lessons.saint: Zita of Lucca: a domestic servant who sanctified every chore.
misc: “My job is just a way to make money.”
lessons.mem: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 2:15 (“to till it and keep it”). Ask: “Was work a punishment or a gift?” Work existed before the fall; toil was added by sin.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain a Christian view of work and apply it to a career path.

script.open: Ask, “What do you spend most of your week doing? What would it mean to say that this is a vocation?” Take answers. “Many people think of vocation as only priests and nuns. The Church says every kind of work can be holy.”
teach: Say: “Genesis 2:15: ‘The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.’ Work is part of God’s plan, before the fall. After the fall, it became toilsome (Genesis 3:17-19), but it remains good. Jesus himself worked as a carpenter. Paul: ‘If anyone will not work, let him not eat.’ (2 Thessalonians 3:10) John Paul II’s Laborem Exercens (1981) teaches that work is ‘a fundamental dimension of human existence’ and that it is for the person, not the person for work. Through work we share in God’s creative activity, support ourselves and our families, serve the community and develop our gifts.”

Say: “The Church also teaches about gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul describes charisms, gifts of the Holy Spirit for building up the Church: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, interpretation; and in Romans 12, teaching, service, encouragement, giving, leading, mercy. ‘To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.’ Everyone has gifts. Talents (Matthew 25:14-30) are given to be used and multiplied, not buried. A calling to a career involves our gifts, interests, values, opportunities and the needs of others. Parable of the talents shows that God expects us to risk and invest.”

Say: “How can work be holy? Offer it to God in a morning offering. Do it well, with integrity, honesty and excellence (Colossians 3:23: ‘Whatever your task, work heartily, as serving the Lord and not men’). Treat colleagues with dignity. Avoid dishonest gain. Set limits: keep Sunday, avoid being a slave to work. Use income justly and generously. Josemaría Escrivá taught that ordinary work is a path to holiness. Zita shows that the meaning of work isn’t the status of the task but the love in which it is done. Choose a career asking: Will it let me serve? Will it respect my values and my future family? Vocation is not only what you do but how you live.”
ask: What does Laborem Exercens teach? (Work is for the person; it shares in God’s creative work.)
What is a charism? (A gift of the Spirit for the common good.)
How can work be holy? (Offer it to God, do it well, with integrity and love.)
practice: List five gifts you have (be honest and specific) and ask two others to name one more.
Match one gift to a need in your school, parish or community.
Write a morning offering for your work or studies.
Choose one concrete way to use your gift this month.
script.close: Pray the Morning Offering. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one task well, as a prayer.”

tryit: Assess your gifts honestly.
Match one gift to a need.
Write how work can be prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Zita was born around 1212 in a village in Tuscany, to a poor, devout family. At twelve she was sent to work as a servant in the household of a wealthy cloth merchant, the Fatinelli family, in Lucca, and she stayed in that house for the rest of her life, about forty-eight years.
She was conscientious and did every task as if for God. She rose early to attend Mass before beginning work, and prayed as she worked. Her fellow servants resented her; the master and mistress were severe at first. Zita bore it patiently. She gave away food to the poor from the table, to the point of trouble, and once, according to a story, when found out with bread in her apron, it was turned to flowers. Another story is that while she prayed, angels baked the household’s bread.
In time, the family grew to respect and love her. She became the trusted head of the household. She died in 1272. She is patron of domestic workers.

units.title: Faith and culture
units.eq: How does faith meet the modern world?

lessons.title: Faith and science
lessons.idea: Faith and reason are two wings by which the human spirit rises to the truth (Fides et Ratio). Because God is the author of both, genuine science and faith cannot conflict. When they seem to, we have misread one of them.
lessons.question: Is evolution compatible with faith?
lessons.activity: “Study Fides et Ratio” (45 min). Students read excerpts from John Paul II’s encyclical (1998) and summarize: the dangers of fideism and rationalism, the role of philosophy, and the call to seek truth. Then take a case (Galileo, evolution, the Big Bang and Fr. Lemaître) and show how faith and science interact.
teach: “Even though faith is above reason, there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason” (CCC 159). The same God who reveals mysteries has endowed the human spirit with reason.
Methodical research in every branch of knowledge, when carried out in a truly scientific manner, “never conflicts with faith” (CCC 159; Gaudium et Spes 36).
Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, proposed the Big Bang theory. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics. Many scientists have been believers.
Scientism, the claim that only empirical science yields truth, is itself a philosophical position, not a scientific result.
talk: How do you respond to claims of conflict?
What is the role of philosophy?
quiz: A believer says, “If I just follow the science, I must give up faith.” What does the Church’s teaching in Fides et Ratio say?|Reason is the enemy of faith|Faith and reason are two wings; truth cannot contradict truth|Science and faith have separate truths that conflict|Only faith matters|1|CCC 159; Fides et Ratio opens with the two-wings image.

Scientism is the claim that…|Faith can answer scientific questions|Science is a good gift|Only what can be measured empirically is real or knowable|Scientists should be religious|2|It is itself a philosophical claim that science cannot prove.

Which person shows that a Catholic priest has contributed to modern science?|Descartes, a bishop|Darwin, a monk|Galileo, who was a priest|Georges Lemaître, who proposed the big bang|3|Lemaître was a Belgian priest and physicist; Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics.
lessons.saint: Blessed Nicolas Steno: a Danish scientist who founded modern geology and then became a bishop.
lessons.mem: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.” (Psalm 19:1)
lessons.hook: Show the opening line of Fides et Ratio: “Faith and reason are like two wings.” Ask: “What happens to a bird with one wing?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how faith and reason relate and respond to an alleged conflict.

script.open: Write two headlines on the board: ‘Scientist finds God in the lab’ and ‘Science proves faith false.’ Ask which one you would expect to see in the news, and why. Use the answer to open the real question.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that faith and reason cannot contradict, because the same God is the author of both. The First Vatican Council: ‘Though faith is above reason, there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason. Since the same God who reveals mysteries and infuses faith has bestowed the light of reason on the human mind, God cannot deny himself, nor can truth ever be in opposition to truth.’ (Dei Filius, as quoted in CCC 159) John Paul II: ‘Science can purify religion from error and superstition. Religion can purify science from idolatry and false absolutes.’ Both seek truth, using different methods and asking different questions.”

Say: “Historical myths. The Galileo case (1633) was real, but is often exaggerated: it was a clash over the interpretation of Scripture and the state of evidence, not the Church’s opposition to science. The Church was a major patron of science: universities, observatories (the Vatican Observatory), priest-scientists like Copernicus (a canon), Mendel (a friar who founded genetics), Lemaître (the Big Bang), and Steno. ‘The Middle Ages believed in a flat earth’ is false; educated people knew the earth was round. The idea of a permanent war between faith and science comes largely from the 19th-century ‘conflict thesis’ and is rejected by historians of science. Real tensions exist: some people take Genesis as a science textbook (fundamentalism), and some use science to claim there is no God (scientism).”

Say: “Hard questions today. Evolution: the Church allows that the human body may have evolved, but each soul is directly created by God (Pius XII, Humani Generis; John Paul II, 1996 message; Benedict XVI). The Church rejects materialistic evolution as a total worldview. Origins: the Big Bang and the age of the universe are compatible with creation, which is about the dependence of everything on God, not just the first moment. The mind: neuroscience studies brain activity, but the Church teaches that the spiritual soul is not reducible to matter. Miracles: not violations of nature, but events beyond nature’s power, signs. Creation is rational and ordered, and this is why science works. Many scientists believe in God: Francis Collins, John Lennox, George Coyne. Science investigates how; faith asks why. Be humble about both.”
ask: Can truth contradict truth? (No; the same God is author of both.)
Name a scientist who was a Catholic priest or religious. (Steno, Mendel, Lemaître.)
What does the Church say about evolution? (The body may have evolved; the soul is directly created.)
practice: List ten statements that people make about science and religion (e.g., ‘The Church burned scientists,’ ‘Evolution disproves God’).
Sort them: myth, partly true, real question.
Pick one real question and write how a Catholic scientist might answer.
Write a one-paragraph principle: how faith and science relate.
script.close: Pray Psalm 19:1-4 or Psalm 8. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the biography of a Catholic scientist.”

tryit: Sort claims of conflict between faith and science.
Mark which are real questions and which are myths.
Write the Church’s principles.
lessons.saintStory:
Niels Stensen, or Nicolas Steno, was born in Copenhagen in 1638 to a Lutheran family. He was a brilliant student of anatomy. At twenty-seven he discovered the duct of the parotid gland, still called Steno’s duct. He showed that the heart is a muscle. In Florence, studying a shark’s head, he noticed that its teeth resembled “tongue stones” found in rocks, and concluded that rocks had been formed by layers of sediment, and that fossils were remains of once-living creatures. He formulated principles of layering, which became the foundation of geology.
At the height of his scientific career, he experienced a spiritual crisis. He studied the faith and in 1667 was received into the Catholic Church in Florence. He gave up science, was ordained a priest in 1675, and was named a bishop in 1677 to serve the Church in northern Germany and Scandinavia. He lived in great poverty, giving away his possessions and his bishop’s ring.
He died in 1686, at forty-eight. He was beatified in 1988. He shows that a scientist can be a man of faith.

lessons.title: Atheism and secularism
lessons.idea: The Church engages unbelief with honesty and charity. Atheism takes many forms: practical atheism, agnosticism, scientism, and secularism. The Church listens, asks why, and offers the reasons for hope. Believers also bear some responsibility for unbelief.
lessons.question: How do we respond to atheism?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (45 min). Teams argue the question “Can one be good without God?” One side takes a Christian view of grounding morality in God; the other presents a secular case and its strengths. Afterwards they list where they found common ground and where the real disagreement lies.
teach: Atheism is one of the gravest problems of our time (CCC 2123–2126; Gaudium et Spes 19–21). It has diverse forms: denial of God, agnosticism, indifference, scientism, ideologies.
Believers can contribute to unbelief when they present a distorted image of God (CCC 2125). A credible witness and genuine dialogue are needed.
Secularism separates public life from faith; the Church distinguishes healthy secularity (autonomy of earthly affairs) from secularism (excluding God).
Engage with respect. Listen to what people have suffered or doubted. Offer reasons: the contingency of the world, the moral law, beauty, Christ.
quiz: The Catechism says believers can contribute to atheism when they…|Present a distorted picture of God or fail to live the faith credibly (CCC 2125)|Pray too much|Study philosophy|Attend Mass|0|CCC 2125.
Practical atheism means…|Worshiping nature|Denying God by argument|Being agnostic by principle|Living as if God does not matter, even without denying him|3|CCC 2125.

Paul’s approach in the Areopagus (Acts 17) models…|Silence about Christ|Avoiding philosophy|Starting from what listeners already believe and then proclaiming the Gospel|Condemning the crowd first|2|He cites their altar and their poets before announcing the resurrection.
lessons.life: Listen to a skeptic with charity.
lessons.saint: G. K. Chesterton: a journalist who argued his way from doubt into the Church and kept laughing.
lessons.mem: “Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.” (1 Peter 3:15)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 17:22–31. Ask: “How does Paul begin his speech to the Athenians? What does he start from?” He starts from their own search.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three forms of unbelief and how to engage each charitably.

script.open: Read a short quotation from a well-known atheist, such as a line from Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens, and then one from a believer. Ask the class to say, in their own words, what each person cares about.
teach: Say: “Atheism is the denial of God’s existence. The Catechism (2123-2128) distinguishes: practical atheism (living as if God doesn’t exist), theoretical atheism (denying God, sometimes based on science, suffering, the problem of evil, or hypocrisy), agnosticism (we cannot know), and indifferentism. The Church says atheism ‘can have various origins’; believers can bear some responsibility ‘to the extent that they neglect their formation in the faith, or present its teaching in a misleading way, or even fail in their religious, moral, or social life.’ (CCC 2125) The Church doesn’t treat atheists as enemies; Vatican II’s Gaudium et Spes calls for dialogue with them.”

Say: “Common arguments and replies. ‘Science has explained everything’: science describes how the world works; it does not answer why there is something rather than nothing, why the laws exist, or the meaning of life. ‘Evil proves there is no God’: this is the strongest argument; the Church replies that God permits evil because of freedom, brings good from it, and in Christ shares our suffering. ‘Religion causes wars’: some conflicts involve religion, but the worst atrocities of the 20th century were committed by atheist regimes, and much of religion’s impact is charity. ‘Religious people are hypocrites’: true, but this speaks of human sin, not God’s existence. ‘I can be good without God’: yes, people can be moral, but the question is the grounding of morality and meaning.’”

Say: “Secularism is the view that public life should be separate from religion, or that religion is a private matter. Healthy secularity respects freedom of conscience and the autonomy of earthly things. But secularism as ideology wants to exclude faith from the public square or from any claim on truth. Features of modern secularism: individualism (me first), consumerism, relativism (‘there’s no truth’), and a loss of transcendence. Benedict XVI called this the ‘dictatorship of relativism.’ Many people are ‘nones’ (no religious affiliation), and the fastest-growing group is those raised in the faith who leave. The Church’s response: the New Evangelization. Give witness, ask good questions, offer beauty, truth and goodness, and answer honestly. Pope Benedict said many ‘seek God without knowing it.’ Chesterton’s laughter is part of it.”
ask: What are practical and theoretical atheism? (Living as if there is no God; claiming there is none.)
How do believers contribute to unbelief? (By poor witness, formation or example.)
What is relativism? (The view that there’s no objective truth.)
practice: Write the strongest argument for atheism in your own words, as fairly as you can.
Write the best reply.
List what secular culture offers and what it cannot provide.
Role-play a respectful conversation between a believer and a skeptic friend.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a skeptical friend what they find most convincing and listen.”

tryit: State the strongest argument for atheism fairly.
Give the strongest Catholic reply.
Say what secularism misses.
lessons.saintStory:
Gilbert Keith Chesterton was born in London in 1874. As a student, he flirted with skepticism and even the occult, and was depressed. He recovered and decided that existence was a gift, and that gratitude was the right response. He became a journalist, poet and novelist, a large man with a cape and a sword stick, known for his wit and paradoxes. He wrote around eighty books and thousands of essays.
His book Orthodoxy (1908) describes his journey to belief as like an explorer who sails to discover a new land and finds he has landed on his own country’s shore. He wrote the Father Brown mysteries featuring a priest-detective. He debated George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells with good humor. He was received into the Catholic Church in 1922.
He died in 1936. Pius XI named him Defender of the Faith. A cause for his canonization has been opened. He wrote, “The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.”

lessons.title: Pluralism and religious freedom
lessons.idea: The Church affirms religious freedom as a right rooted in human dignity: no one may be forced to act against conscience or prevented from acting in accord with it, within just limits. Faith must be free, and the Church defends this freedom for all people.
lessons.question: What is religious freedom?
lessons.activity: “Study Dignitatis Humanae” (45 min). Students read key paragraphs (DH 2–4) and summarize the argument. They then map current cases of religious persecution and restriction around the world and discuss what believers and governments should do.
teach: Vatican II’s Dignitatis Humanae (1965): the right to religious freedom is based on the dignity of the human person (CCC 2104–2109). Faith is a free act and cannot be coerced.
This right is for everyone, including non-Christians. The state must protect it, within just public order. The Church also claims freedom to carry out her mission.
The teaching develops earlier practice: the Church acknowledges that coercion in matters of faith was sometimes wrongly used in history.
Religious freedom is increasingly threatened: Christians are among the most persecuted groups worldwide.
talk: Why does the Church defend it?
quiz: According to Dignitatis Humanae, religious freedom is grounded in…|Indifference about truth|The state’s permission|The dignity of the human person, who must not be coerced in matters of conscience|The majority’s will|2|CCC 2106; DH 2.

Which statement is true?|The Church has never changed its practice on coercion|The Church teaches that all religions are equally true|The Church teaches that no one may be forced to act against conscience in religion, within just public order|Religious freedom means faith is private only|2|The teaching is firm and its application has developed.

“My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36) is cited because it shows…|Christ’s mission is not advanced by force|Faith must be hidden|Christians should avoid politics|The state has no authority|0|The Gospel is proposed, not imposed.
lessons.saint: Blessed Alojzije Stepinac: an archbishop who sheltered the persecuted and was jailed for refusing to bow to the state.
misc: “Religious freedom means all religions are equally true.”
lessons.mem: “My kingdom is not of this world.” (John 18:36)
lessons.hook: Read John 18:36 (“My kingdom is not of this world”). Ask: “Why did Jesus refuse to fight?” The Gospel is proposed, not imposed.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the foundation of religious freedom and one global application.

script.open: Ask, “Should a government be allowed to forbid a religion? To force one? What about a school requiring a prayer, or a hospital being forced to do something against its faith? Where is the line?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Vatican II’s Dignitatis Humanae (1965), the Declaration on Religious Freedom, taught that ‘the human person has a right to religious freedom. This freedom means that all men are to be immune from coercion on the part of individuals or of social groups and of any human power, in such wise that in matters religious no one is to be forced to act in a manner contrary to his own beliefs. Nor is anyone to be restrained from acting in accordance with his own beliefs, whether privately or publicly, whether alone or in association with others, within due limits.’ This is based on human dignity and the nature of faith, which must be free. This freedom is a civil right, not a claim that all religions are equally true.”

Say: “This was a development in the Church’s expression. In earlier times, in Christendom, the state often enforced religious unity. The Church recognized more clearly that coercion in matters of faith is contrary to dignity (an idea found in Tertullian and Lactantius). John Courtney Murray, an American Jesuit, helped develop the teaching, drawing on the American experience. The Church still teaches that there’s one true religion and that all are bound to seek truth, but that nobody can be forced. Limits: public order and the common good. The state must protect religious freedom, but not necessarily endorse a religion. The Church requests freedom to worship, teach, run institutions, and act in public life according to conscience.”

Say: “Pluralism: modern society includes many religions and worldviews. The Church affirms that Catholics can live in a pluralist society, cooperate with others on common goals, and respect other beliefs. We shouldn’t force our beliefs through coercion, but we should bring our convictions to public debate, with reasoned arguments accessible to all. Real contemporary issues: conscientious objection (healthcare workers, business owners), religious schools and charities, religious persecution abroad (Christians are the most persecuted religious group in the world), blasphemy laws, and public symbols. Religious freedom is under pressure in many countries. Stepinac’s life shows that totalitarian states often see the Church as a rival. The Church defends the freedom of all religions, not only her own.”
ask: What does Dignitatis Humanae teach? (Everyone has the right to religious freedom, free from coercion.)
Does it teach all religions are equally true? (No; it’s about civil freedom.)
What are limits on religious freedom? (Public order and the common good.)
practice: Prepare cases: a Catholic pharmacist and a prescription; a school board and a prayer; a country that bans conversion; a Catholic charity and a government requirement.
For each, decide what religious freedom requires and what the common good might limit.
Write a principle for a pluralist society.
Share and debate with respect.
script.close: Pray for persecuted Christians and all who suffer for conscience. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look up a place where religious freedom is restricted.”

tryit: Distinguish religious freedom from relativism.
State what the state may and may not do.
Apply it to a case.
lessons.saintStory:
Alojzije Stepinac was born in 1898 in Croatia, the eighth of eight children in a farming family. He served in the First World War, then studied for the priesthood in Rome. In 1937 he was named archbishop of Zagreb at thirty-nine. During the Second World War, Croatia was ruled by the fascist Ustaše regime, which persecuted Serbs, Jews and Roma. Stepinac spoke against it in sermons and letters. He sheltered Jews, helped hundreds escape, and condemned racial laws and the killing of civilians.
When the communists took power in Yugoslavia, he refused to break with Rome and set up a national church, and protested the persecution of the Church. In 1946 he was arrested and put on trial in a show trial, accused of collaboration with the fascists. He was sentenced to sixteen years of hard labor. After five years in prison, he was put under house arrest in his home village, where he stayed until his death in 1960.
Pope Pius XII made him a cardinal in 1953. John Paul II beatified him in 1998. His case remains debated by historians.

lessons.title: Subsidiarity and participation
lessons.idea: Subsidiarity holds that decisions should be made at the lowest level able to handle them, with higher bodies helping but not replacing. Participation means every person has the right and duty to contribute to the common good. These two principles protect freedom and community.
lessons.question: What is subsidiarity?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (40 min). Provide a scenario (a school district, a parish, a city) where a central authority has taken over local decisions, or where local groups are neglecting a need. Students apply subsidiarity: who should decide? Who should help? Where is intervention justified?
teach: Subsidiarity: “a community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, depriving the latter of its functions” (CCC 1883; Pius XI, Quadragesimo Anno).
It also requires higher bodies to help when lower ones cannot cope (CCC 1884–1885). It guards against both individualism and collectivism.
Participation: all citizens have a right and duty to take part in public life (CCC 1913–1917). Voting, serving, volunteering, informed engagement.
Show examples: the family before the state, the parish before the diocese, local charity before national programs.
talk: How does it apply to school?
quiz: The principle of subsidiarity says…|Decisions should be made at the lowest level able to act well, with higher bodies helping when needed|All decisions belong to the largest body|Local groups may ignore the law|The state should do everything|0|CCC 1883–1885.

Which situation violates subsidiarity?|A national agency takes over a function a local community could perform well|A city helps a school in need|A diocese coordinates parishes|A parish asks a family to help|0|The higher body replaces what lower bodies can do.
Participation in public life is…|A right and a duty according to one’s role (CCC 1913–1917)|Optional for Christians|Reserved to officials|Forbidden to clergy only|0|CCC 1913–1917.
lessons.saint: Pierre Toussaint: a former slave from Haiti who became a successful hairdresser in New York and gave away his money.
lessons.mem: “Just as the body is one and has many members… so it is with Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Corinthians 12:14–20. Ask: “What if the head did everything and the hands did nothing?” Introduce subsidiarity.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define subsidiarity and apply it to a concrete case.

script.open: Describe a small problem, such as a broken swing in a park. Ask who should fix it: the family, the neighbors, the town, the state, or the nation. Take a quick poll and a reason from each camp.
teach: Say: “Subsidiarity is a key principle of Catholic social teaching. Pius XI in Quadragesimo Anno (1931): ‘It is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.’ The Catechism: ‘A community of a higher order should not interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, depriving the latter of its functions, but rather should support it in case of need.’ (CCC 1883) The family, local communities and voluntary associations (the ‘mediating structures’) should be respected. The state should help, not replace. At the same time, higher levels should step in when lower ones cannot.”

Say: “Subsidiarity has two sides: it limits intervention, and it requires help. If a family is struggling, the neighborhood, parish and charity should help; if they can’t, the city, state or nation should. It protects freedom and responsibility, and recognizes that decisions are best made by those closest to the situation. It opposes both excessive centralization (totalitarianism, bureaucratic over-control) and a negligent neglect of the vulnerable. In the Church, subsidiarity applies too: the diocese and parish have their roles, and the Pope does not micromanage. Also in economics: small businesses, cooperatives and local solutions.”

Say: “Participation: ‘It is a requirement of human dignity that people take an active part in public life.’ (GS 75) Everyone has a right and a duty to contribute to the common good: voting, serving on boards, volunteering, paying taxes, running for office, speaking up. Ways Pierre Toussaint participated: through his work, giving, and building institutions. Obstacles: poverty, discrimination, apathy, cynicism. The Church encourages Catholics to engage in politics from their conscience. She doesn’t tell people how to vote, but forms conscience on principles: the dignity of life, family, the poor, the common good. In the U.S., Faithful Citizenship sets this out. For young people: register to vote, learn the issues, volunteer locally, join a community group. Citizenship is a form of charity.”
ask: What is subsidiarity? (Decisions should be made at the lowest competent level, with higher levels helping when needed.)
What is participation? (Everyone’s right and duty to take part in public life.)
Whom did Pierre Toussaint help? (Orphans, the sick, refugees, enslaved people, the Church.)
practice: Choose three problems: a school bullying issue, a food shortage in the town, a national healthcare policy.
For each, decide who should act first and who should help.
Write one way you can participate in public life this year.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help me to do my part for the common good.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find out how to register to vote or join a community group.”

tryit: Apply subsidiarity to an example.
Identify who should decide.
Describe a way to participate.
lessons.saintStory:
Pierre Toussaint was born in 1766, enslaved in Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). He was taught to read by his owner’s family, and was brought to New York in 1787 by his mistress, Madame Bérard. There he trained as a hairdresser and became popular with wealthy women. When her husband died, leaving her poor, Pierre supported her with his earnings, until she died in 1807 and freed him.
After being freed, he continued to work hard and prospered. He and his wife Juliette, who was also freed, lived modestly. He gave generously: to orphans, to the sick during yellow fever epidemics, to refugees; he bought freedom for others; and he helped raise money for the first Catholic cathedral in New York, St. Patrick’s on Mott Street. He went to Mass every day.
He died in 1853. He is buried in the crypt at the new St. Patrick’s Cathedral. He was declared Venerable in 1996. His life shows the dignity of work and the power of a person who does good in his own sphere.

lessons.title: Economic life
lessons.idea: Economic life exists to serve the person. The Church teaches the dignity of work, a just wage, the right to private property with a social purpose, the rights of workers to organize, and care for the poor. Rerum Novarum began a long tradition of social teaching on economics.
lessons.question: What is a just wage?
lessons.activity: “Reading Rerum Novarum summary” (45 min). Students read a summary of Leo XIII’s 1891 encyclical. They identify: what it rejects (socialism’s abolition of property, unregulated capitalism), what it affirms (private property, a just wage, unions). Then apply to a modern case: gig work, minimum wage, remote work.
teach: Work is for the person; the economy must serve people (CCC 2426–2428). Economic life is subject to moral law (CCC 2423–2425).
Just wages enable a family to live with dignity (CCC 2434). Workers have the right to strike in just circumstances and to form unions (CCC 2435).
Private property is legitimate but has a “universal destination of goods” (CCC 2402–2406). Charity does not replace justice.
Later documents (Quadragesimo Anno, Centesimus Annus, Caritas in Veritate) address globalization, markets and the common good.
talk: What is the universal destination of goods?
What is the role of business?
quiz: Catholic social teaching about private property holds that…|It belongs only to the state|It is evil|It is legitimate yet bound by the universal destination of goods|It is absolute|2|CCC 2402–2406.

Rerum Novarum (1891) is notable because it…|Rejected all labor unions|Defended workers’ rights, a just wage and private property against both socialism and unrestrained markets|Was addressed only to priests|Endorsed communism|1|Leo XIII.

A just wage is, in the Church’s view, one that…|The market sets, whatever it is|Allows a worker to support a family with dignity (CCC 2434)|Equals what the employer likes|Is the same for everyone in all jobs|1|CCC 2434.
lessons.life: Read the opening of Rerum Novarum.
lessons.saint: Blessed Giuseppe Toniolo: an economics professor and father of seven who taught that economics must serve people.
lessons.mem: “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” (James 5:4)
lessons.hook: Read James 5:1–6 on wages held back. Ask: “What does James condemn? What does it say about how God sees workers?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state four principles of Catholic economic teaching.

script.open: Hold up a pair of sneakers or a phone. Say, “Where was this made, by whom, for what wage?” Give pairs three minutes to guess and then look up one fact on the label or online.
teach: Say: “Gaudium et Spes 63: ‘Man is the source, the focus and the end of all economic and social life.’ The Church teaches that the economy exists for people, not people for the economy. The Compendium of the Social Doctrine states principles for economic life. Work has priority over capital: work is an expression of the person. Just wage: ‘The just wage is the legitimate fruit of work.’ (CCC 2434) A wage should be enough to support a worker and family in dignity. Rights of workers: safe conditions, rest, the right to organize in unions, fair treatment. Property: private property is legitimate, but with a social purpose. Business: should seek profit, but also serve the community and respect workers. Consumers: have duties too, including avoiding waste and unfair purchases.”

Say: “The Church has criticized various systems. Marxism and communism: denies God, abolishes private property, class struggle; condemned by Pius IX, Leo XIII, Pius XI. Unrestrained capitalism or liberalism: individualism, profit as the only goal, commodifying persons; criticized in Rerum Novarum and Quadragesimo Anno, and by Pope Francis (‘an economy of exclusion’; ‘idolatry of money’). The Church says: no system is perfect. Markets are good for efficiency, but they need moral and legal framework: ‘The market is not automatically just.’ Centesimus Annus (1991) by John Paul II after the fall of communism: affirmed the free market and private enterprise, in a context of strong ethics and law, and criticized consumerism. Caritas in Veritate (2009) by Benedict XVI: the economy needs gratuity and fraternity, not only contracts.”

Say: “Particular questions. Poverty and inequality: the Church teaches preferential concern for the poor. Debt of poor nations and fair trade. Taxes and the role of government: government has a role in justice, but subsidiarity limits. Globalization: benefits and risks. Usury, gambling, advertising and consumerism. Environment. Employers and employees: the duty to treat people as persons. Immigration: the right to emigrate for a decent life; nations have the right to regulate borders for the common good, but must welcome as far as possible. Individual Catholics can disagree on policy while sharing principles. Your own habits: how you spend, save and give. Tithing and almsgiving. Think about what you buy, who made it, and what it costs. Toniolo’s lesson: economics is a moral science; study it.”
ask: What is the economy for? (The person and the common good.)
What is a just wage? (Enough to support a worker and family in dignity.)
What did Centesimus Annus say of the free market? (Good within a moral and legal framework.)
practice: Make a chart comparing communism, unregulated capitalism and the Church’s approach, using three principles: dignity, property, work.
Find one product you use and trace who made it and in what conditions.
Write a personal ‘economic ethic’ of five commitments.
Share one.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give us a just economy that serves all.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Tithe or give a portion of what you earn to the poor.”

tryit: Compare three economic systems by Church principles.
Mark what each gets right and wrong.
Write a just-wage principle.
lessons.saintStory:
Giuseppe Toniolo was born in 1845 in Treviso, Italy, and became a professor of economics at the University of Pisa. He was a devout Catholic, a layman, and the father of seven children. At a time when many Catholic intellectuals felt cut off from the modern world, he insisted that Catholics should study economics and social sciences seriously, and that economic life should be guided by ethics.
He founded the Catholic Union for Social Studies in 1889, which organized the Catholic Social Weeks in Italy, and he influenced Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum. He promoted cooperatives, rural banks, workers’ unions, and fair wages. He wrote that the economy should serve human beings, and he argued against both unregulated liberalism and socialism.
He lived a simple life, going to Mass every day, and loved his family. He died in 1918 and was beatified in 2012. He shows that economics can be a path to holiness.

lessons.title: War and peace
lessons.idea: The Church promotes peace as “the tranquility of order” and holds that war is always a failure of humanity. She also teaches that use of force may be legitimate in strictly limited conditions of defense, when just war criteria are met. Peacemakers are blessed.
lessons.question: What is just war?
lessons.activity: “Study” (45 min). Students study the just war criteria (CCC 2309): lasting, grave damage by an aggressor; all other means impractical; serious prospects of success; no greater evils produced. They then evaluate a historical case against the criteria and discuss the role of conscientious objectors.
teach: Peace is “the tranquility of order” (Augustine; CCC 2304) and requires justice and charity. “Blessed are the peacemakers” (CCC 2305).

All citizens and governments are obliged to avoid war; yet governments have the right of legitimate defense (CCC 2308–2309). The conditions for just war are strict; the means must also be just (CCC 2312–2314).
Conscientious objection is respected (CCC 2311). Arms race, terrorism, torture and indiscriminate destruction are gravely wrong (CCC 2314–2317).
Recent popes have asked whether war can still be justified given modern weapons. The Church supports nonviolent peacemaking.
quiz: Which is among the conditions for a just war (CCC 2309)?|Lasting, grave and certain damage inflicted by an aggressor, with all other means shown impractical|The enemy is of another religion|The ruler wishes it|It would be profitable|0|CCC 2309.

The Church’s teaching on conscientious objection is that…|It is always wrong|The law should provide for those who refuse to bear arms, if they serve in another way (CCC 2311)|It applies only to priests|It is required of all|1|CCC 2311.
Peace, in the Catechism’s phrase, is…|The mere absence of war|The tranquility of order (CCC 2304)|Impossible on earth|A feeling|1|Augustine’s definition; peace requires justice and charity.
lessons.saint: Maximilian of Tebessa: a twenty-one-year-old who refused to be a soldier and was beheaded.
misc: “Just war means any war our side declares just.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:9: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” Ask: “Is peace the same as the absence of war?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to list the just war criteria and apply them to a case.

script.open: Ask, “Is it ever right to use force? To go to war? To refuse to fight? What is the best argument on each side?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church’s teaching on war and peace: the Catechism 2302-2317. Peace is not just the absence of war, but ‘the tranquility of order’ (Augustine), the work of justice and charity. ‘Blessed are the peacemakers.’ (Matthew 5:9) Anger and hatred are against the fifth commandment. War is always an evil, but the Church holds that governments have the right and duty of legitimate defense once peaceful efforts have failed. Pacifism is a legitimate personal vocation for those who choose non-violence, as Maximilian did, and the Church honors conscientious objectors. But the Church does not teach that all use of force is wrong.”

Say: “Just war theory, from Augustine and Aquinas. The conditions for legitimate defense by military force are: the damage inflicted by the aggressor must be lasting, grave and certain; all other means must have been shown to be impractical or ineffective; there must be serious prospects of success; the use of arms must not produce evils graver than the evil to be eliminated. (CCC 2309) Also: just cause, legitimate authority, right intention. In conduct (jus in bello): noncombatants must be protected; the means must be proportionate; some acts are never allowed: indiscriminate destruction of cities, torture, targeting civilians. Vatican II condemned total war: ‘Any act of war aimed indiscriminately at the destruction of entire cities or extensive areas along with their populations is a crime against God and man.’ (GS 80)”

Say: “Modern questions. Nuclear weapons: the Church condemns their use, and has been skeptical of deterrence as a long-term solution; Pope Francis has called possession of nuclear weapons immoral. Terrorism: always wrong. The arms race: ‘an utterly treacherous trap for humanity.’ (GS 81) Humanitarian intervention: ‘responsibility to protect.’ The Pope’s role: John Paul II opposed the 2003 Iraq war. Military service: Catholics may serve honorably; soldiers must refuse unlawful orders. Peace-building: dialogue, justice, development, forgiveness. ‘Peace is the work of justice’ (Isaiah 32:17). Paul VI: ‘If you want peace, work for justice.’ Peace begins in our hearts and homes: how we handle conflicts, forgive and speak. Pope Francis: ‘War is always a defeat for humanity.’ Pray, fast and act for peace.”
ask: Does the Church teach that war is always wrong? (No; she teaches legitimate defense under strict conditions.)
Name three conditions of just war. (Just cause, last resort, probability of success, proportionality.)
What does the Church say of conscientious objectors? (Honors them.)
practice: Choose a historical or current conflict.
Test it against the just war criteria in a table: which are met, which not.
Write a paragraph on what the Church would ask for in this case.
Write one concrete act of peacemaking you can do in your own life.
script.close: Pray the Prayer of Saint Francis or the Litany for Peace. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make peace with someone with whom you have a conflict.”

tryit: Test a case against the just war criteria.
Mark which fail.
Write what peacemaking asks of you.
lessons.saintStory:
Maximilian was a young man in Numidia, in North Africa, in AD 295. He was the son of a veteran soldier named Fabius Victor, and as such was required to enlist in the Roman army. His father brought him before the proconsul Dion in Tebessa (Theveste) for the military enrollment. The record of the trial, called the Acts of Maximilian, is one of the oldest documents about Christians and military service.
When the recruiting officer was about to put a lead seal around his neck, the sign of enlistment, Maximilian said, “I cannot serve as a soldier. I cannot do evil. I am a Christian.” The proconsul said, “Serve and receive the seal.” Maximilian said, “I will not receive the seal. I already have the seal of Christ.”
They tried to persuade him, and his father urged him to comply. He refused. The proconsul sentenced him to death. Maximilian said, “Thanks be to God.” He was beheaded on March 12, 295. His father returned home, giving thanks that he had given such a gift to God. He is considered the patron of conscientious objectors.

lessons.title: The sanctity of life
lessons.idea: Every human life is sacred from conception to natural death because each person is made in God’s image. Direct abortion and the intentional killing of the innocent are gravely wrong, and the Church calls for help for mothers, families and everyone in need.
lessons.question: Why from conception?
lessons.activity: “Research” (45 min). Students research the science of fetal development, local pregnancy-help services and Church teaching (Evangelium Vitae). They produce a one-page brief that presents the Church’s argument, how to respond to common objections, and ways to support women in crisis. Respect those with painful experiences.
teach: Human life is sacred from conception until natural death (CCC 2258, 2270–2271). Abortion is a grave moral evil (CCC 2271); formal cooperation incurs excommunication (CCC 2272).
Science: a unique human organism with its own DNA begins at fertilization. The Church’s argument is based on human dignity, not only on faith.
The Church also teaches compassion: Project Rachel offers healing for post-abortion pain; pregnancy centers and parishes can support women (CCC 2274–2275).
Respect for life also includes the poor, migrants, the disabled and the elderly (Evangelium Vitae 87).
talk: How do we respond with compassion?
quiz: The Church’s case against abortion rests mainly on…|The dignity of every human person from conception, which reason can recognize, and the commandment against killing the innocent|A single verse|Politics alone|Medical preference|0|CCC 2270–2271.

Which response best reflects the Church’s pastoral approach after an abortion?|Mercy and healing available through Confession and ministries such as Project Rachel (CCC 2279)|Despair|Silence|Blame|0|The Church offers forgiveness and accompaniment.

Which is part of defending life “from conception to natural death”?|Ignoring the dying|Only opposing abortion|Also caring for the poor, the sick, migrants and the elderly|Leaving it to the state|2|Evangelium Vitae links all.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth: the first person to call Mary’s unborn child Lord.
misc: “The Church only cares about unborn life.”
lessons.mem: “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb.” (Psalm 139:13)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16. Ask: “What does this say about when a person begins to matter to God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present the Church’s case and how to support women in crisis.

script.open: Show a first ultrasound image. Say, “Describe what you see. No arguments yet, only observations.” Collect descriptions, then ask what words people use for this stage of life, and why those words matter.
teach: Say: “The Church’s teaching on the sanctity of life is rooted in Scripture, reason and tradition. Scripture: ‘You shall not kill’ (Exodus 20:13); God knows us in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5, Psalm 139:13-16); Elizabeth’s encounter (Luke 1:39-45); the Incarnation itself, where the Son of God began as an embryo. Tradition: the Didache and Letter of Barnabas (first century) forbid abortion; the Fathers, including Tertullian, Basil and Chrysostom, condemned it. The Catechism: ‘Since the first century the Church has affirmed the moral evil of every procured abortion. This teaching has not changed and remains unchangeable. Direct abortion, that is to say, abortion willed either as an end or a means, is gravely contrary to the moral law.’ (CCC 2271)”

Say: “The reasoning. Biology: at fertilization, a new, genetically distinct, living human organism comes into being. It is not a part of the mother’s body; it has its own DNA, sex and development. It develops continuously; there is no point at which it becomes human, though it becomes more developed. Philosophy: the question is not ‘when does it become a person?’ with criteria like consciousness, viability or independence, because these criteria would also exclude newborns, the sleeping, or the severely disabled. The Church argues that personhood is a property of what a thing is, not what it can do. The prudential argument: even if one were unsure, we should not risk killing. Evangelium Vitae (1995) of John Paul II: ‘the unconditional respect for the right to life of every innocent person.’”

Say: “Responses to hard cases. Rape: a horrific crime; the woman needs compassion and care; the child is innocent, and punishing the child does not heal the crime. Health of the mother: if a pregnant woman has a life-threatening condition, treatment aiming to cure the mother (e.g., removing a cancerous uterus, treating an ectopic pregnancy) is permitted even if the child dies as a side effect. Direct abortion is never allowed. Fetal abnormality: every life has value; perinatal hospice and support exist. Poverty: the Church supports mothers with material help. Legal question: the Church holds that law should protect the unborn and doesn’t see abortion as only a private matter; the debate involves political prudence. Healing: Project Rachel, confession, and compassion. Pro-life means pro-woman and pro-child: Elizabeth and Mary supported each other. Being pro-life also means supporting the elderly, the poor, the disabled, and ending violence.”
ask: What does the Church teach about abortion? (It is gravely wrong; life begins at conception.)
What is the difference between abortion and treatment of a cancerous uterus? (Abortion directly intends the child’s death; the treatment aims to cure the mother.)
What does being pro-life mean fully? (Supporting mothers, children, the disabled and the vulnerable.)
practice: Make a table: Science / Philosophy / Scripture and Tradition / Church’s conclusion.
Write the strongest objection you have heard and a charitable reply.
List five forms of practical support for a woman in a crisis pregnancy.
Choose one to support concretely.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary for mothers, unborn children and all affected. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a mother in a difficult pregnancy.”

tryit: List what science says about early human development.
List what philosophy asks.
State the Church’s conclusion and its basis.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth was the wife of the priest Zechariah and a relative of Mary. Both were righteous before God, but they had no child and were old. In the Temple, Zechariah was told by the angel Gabriel that Elizabeth would bear a son, to be named John, who would prepare the way for the Lord. Zechariah doubted and was struck silent. Elizabeth conceived and hid herself for five months, saying, “Thus the Lord has done to me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men.”
In her sixth month, Mary, who had just conceived by the Holy Spirit, traveled to the hill country of Judea to visit her. When Mary greeted her, the child in Elizabeth’s womb leaped, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She cried out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”
Before any ultrasound, Elizabeth recognized an unborn child as “my Lord” and her own child as responding with joy. The Church sees in this scene the dignity of life in the womb.

lessons.title: End of life
lessons.idea: Euthanasia and assisted suicide are morally unacceptable because they directly end a life. The Church also allows refusing burdensome treatment and strongly supports palliative care. Suffering has meaning in Christ, and the dying deserve accompaniment.
lessons.question: What is dignified death?
lessons.activity: “Case studies” (45 min). Present three cases: a terminally ill patient requesting assisted suicide, a family deciding on withdrawing ventilators, a hospice patient receiving palliative sedation. Students analyze using the distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means and between intending death and accepting it.
teach: Euthanasia — an action or omission that of itself or by intention causes death in order to eliminate suffering — is morally unacceptable (CCC 2277). Assisted suicide is also gravely wrong (CCC 2282).
Discontinuing disproportionate or burdensome treatment is legitimate (CCC 2278). Pain relief, even if it shortens life, is acceptable if death is not intended (CCC 2279).
Palliative care is a preferred form of charity. Hospice care honors the dying.
Suffering is not good, but united to Christ’s Passion it can be redemptive (CCC 1521, 1505). Accompany the dying with love, presence and the sacraments.
talk: What is ordinary vs extraordinary care?
How do we accompany the dying?
quiz: Which is morally acceptable according to the Catechism?|Direct euthanasia to relieve pain|Refusing disproportionate or burdensome treatment (CCC 2278)|Assisted suicide|Intentionally ending life with an overdose|1|CCC 2277–2279.

Palliative care that relieves pain even if it may shorten life is acceptable when…|The aim is to cause death|The patient is old|Death is not willed or intended and the means are proportionate|It is secret|2|CCC 2279.

Why does the Church say suffering can have meaning?|Because it is unavoidable|Because pain is good|Because united with Christ’s Passion it can be redemptive, while we still work to relieve it|Because God sends it to punish|2|CCC 1521.
lessons.saint: Aloysius Gonzaga: a Jesuit novice who died at twenty-three caring for plague victims.
misc: “The Church requires keeping people alive at all costs.”
lessons.mem: “Jesus wept.” (John 11:35)
lessons.hook: Read John 11, the raising of Lazarus. Ask: “What does Jesus do at the tomb? What does he feel?” He weeps. The Church does not minimize suffering.
lessons.assess: Ask students to distinguish euthanasia from refusal of burdensome treatment with examples.

script.open: Be gentle. Say, “Many of us have lost someone. We’ll treat this topic with care.” Ask, “If someone you loved were dying, what would you want for them?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Review the Church’s teaching (CCC 2276-2279; Evangelium Vitae 64-67; Samaritanus Bonus 2020). Those who are ill or disabled must be cared for. Euthanasia, intentionally causing death to relieve suffering, is always wrong. Assisted suicide is wrong. So-called ‘mercy killing’ is a false mercy. But discontinuing medical procedures that are burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary or disproportionate to the expected outcome is legitimate: it is a refusal of ‘over-zealous’ treatment. One may not choose death, but one may accept it. Ordinary care, such as food, water, hygiene, warmth and companionship, owed to every patient, must not be withdrawn merely to cause death. But if they can’t be assimilated or cause grave burden, they may be limited.”

Say: “The ordinary/extraordinary distinction is about proportion: the benefits versus burdens for this patient. A ventilator for a brief crisis, with hope of recovery, may be ordinary; the same device when the patient is dying and it only prolongs the process, may be disproportionate. Patients (or surrogates) may refuse treatment, with the intent of not prolonging dying, not of causing death. Pain relief: it is permissible to give analgesics even if they might hasten death as a side effect, provided the intention is to relieve pain (double effect). Palliative sedation, used appropriately, for intractable suffering near death, is allowed when not intended to cause death. Brain death and organ donation: the Church accepts the criteria if applied rigorously; organ donation is a generous act, if consent is free and the donor is truly dead.”

Say: “Advance planning. A health care proxy and an advance directive, preferably consistent with Church teaching, help families: they can state wishes about extraordinary measures and name a trusted decision-maker. The Church encourages Catholics to complete them. ‘Do not resuscitate’ orders and POLST forms: can be morally acceptable in some circumstances but should be reviewed. Accompaniment: the Church’s answer to suffering is presence, not elimination. Families should be supported; hospice care can help. The sacraments: Anointing, Viaticum, Confession. Prayer: the Commendation of the Dying, the Rosary. Forgiveness and farewells. Suffering has meaning in union with Christ’s cross, but it’s no good to romanticize pain. John Paul II’s own death in 2005 was a witness: he asked, ‘Let me go to the house of the Father.’ Aloysius gave his life serving the dying.”
ask: Is it ever permitted to stop treatment? (Yes, when it is disproportionate or burdensome, with no intent to cause death.)
What is double effect? (Relieving pain with an unintended risk of shortening life is allowed.)
What is the Church’s answer to suffering? (Presence, care and the sacraments.)
practice: Work in groups on cases: a patient on a ventilator with no hope; a patient refusing chemotherapy; a dying patient in pain; a request for assisted suicide.
For each, decide what the Church would permit and what not.
Write a short list of values for your own advance directive.
Plan how you might support a dying relative.
script.close: Pray the Commendation of the Dying or “Jesus, Mary and Joseph, assist me in my last agony.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Talk with your family about end-of-life wishes.”

tryit: Distinguish ordinary from extraordinary means with cases.
Describe what accompanying the dying involves.
Draft your own advance directive values.
lessons.saintStory:
Aloysius Gonzaga was born in 1568, the oldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione, in northern Italy. He was heir to a title and lands, and grew up in a world of courts and military training. As a boy he was thrilled by war games, and picked up bad language from the soldiers, but was ashamed of it. At about nine, he took a private vow of virginity and became devoted to prayer.
His father opposed his wish to become a priest, wanting him to be a courtier. After years of struggle, Aloysius gave up his claim to the title to his brother, and in 1585, at seventeen, entered the Jesuit novitiate in Rome. In 1591, plague swept the city. The Jesuits opened a hospital for the sick. Aloysius volunteered, washing patients and carrying them on his shoulders from the streets to the hospital.
He caught the plague and was sick for weeks. He died on June 21, 1591, aged twenty-three. He was canonized in 1726 and is patron of youth. His death came from caring for the dying.

lessons.title: Bioethics and technology
lessons.idea: The Church engages new technologies in medicine, biology and computing. She asks of each: Does it respect the dignity of the person? Is the person treated as a subject or as an object? The Church supports science that heals and opposes what degrades human life.
lessons.question: How do we judge technology?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (45 min). Teams debate a motion: “Gene editing of human embryos should be banned.” Use principles: dignity, the common good, the difference between therapy and enhancement. Consider related topics: artificial intelligence, organ donation, stem cells. Write a guiding question to ask of any new technology.
teach: Scientific research is a noble service when it respects human dignity (CCC 2292–2296). Experiments on human beings must respect their rights and consent.
Organ donation is praiseworthy when free and not harmful (CCC 2296). Embryonic stem cell research is wrong since it destroys embryos; adult stem cell research is licit.
Reproductive technologies that separate procreation from the marital act are wrong (CCC 2376–2377). Gene therapy for healing is allowed; eugenics and enhancement raise grave questions.
Artificial intelligence and data raise questions of privacy, work and the human person (Rome Call for AI Ethics; Antiqua et Nova).
talk: How do we judge new technologies?
What is the role of conscience?
quiz: A Catholic test for a new technology starts with the question…|Is it profitable?|Is it new?|Is it legal?|Does it respect the dignity of the person as a subject rather than a thing?|3|CCC 2292–2296.

Which is a licit use of stem cells according to Church teaching?|Cells taken from adult tissue or umbilical cord blood without harming a human embryo|Cells taken by destroying embryos|Any use if it cures|None|0|The Church supports ethical stem-cell research.

Why does the Church warn about “designer babies”?|It dislikes medicine|It is unsafe only|It treats a child as a product to be chosen and risks eugenic discrimination|It forbids all genetics|2|CCC 2377–2379.
lessons.saint: The archangel Raphael: whose name means “God heals,” and who walked beside young Tobias.
misc: “The Church is against all new technology.”
“If we can do it, we should.”
lessons.mem: “Give me wisdom, that sits by your throne.” (Wisdom 9:4)
lessons.hook: Read Wisdom 9:1–6, the prayer for wisdom. Ask: “What does Solomon ask for? Why is wisdom needed with power?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to propose three questions to ask of any new technology.

script.open: Place a smartphone on the table. Say, “In ten years this will look primitive. List three technologies that could change human life as much, for good or ill.” Write them and ask which worry you most.
teach: Say: “Technology is a gift of human intelligence, which participates in God’s creativity. The Church supports medical research and technology that serve human life and dignity. But some things are ethical lines. The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith’s Donum Vitae (1987) and Dignitas Personae (2008) deal with bioethics. The key principles: (1) every human being is a person from conception, with dignity and rights; (2) the person may never be treated merely as a means; (3) procreation belongs in the marital act of love and shouldn’t be replaced by technique; (4) the end doesn’t justify the means. A good question: not only ‘Can we?’ but ‘Should we?’”

Say: “Some current issues. Embryonic stem-cell research: destroys human embryos, and is immoral; adult stem cells, cord blood and induced pluripotent stem cells are ethical. Genetic testing: legitimate for diagnosis and therapy; not legitimate for selecting or discarding embryos or children. Gene therapy: acceptable for healing.
