Genetic enhancement and ‘designer babies’: raises worries of eugenics and inequality. Cloning: reproductive cloning is immoral since it substitutes technique for the act of love and treats the child as a product. Organ transplantation: a good act, provided donors are dead and consent is free; organ trafficking is gravely wrong. Artificial intelligence: raises questions of work, privacy, relationships, truth and war; Pope Francis has called for ‘algor-ethics.’ Transhumanism: the idea of overcoming human limits through technology, risks losing the meaning of the person.”

Say: “How do we think about new technologies? A method: See (what is happening), Judge (by the Gospel and the Church’s teaching: dignity, common good, solidarity, stewardship), Act. Questions: Does it respect life from conception to natural death? Does it treat the person as a subject rather than an object? Does it serve healing or domination? Who benefits and who is left out? Does it protect the vulnerable? Does it respect the family and the natural meaning of the body? Are the means ethical? Raphael’s name reminds us that healing is God’s work, and medicine cooperates in it. Pope Francis wrote in Laudato Si’ of a technocratic paradigm, which tends to see everything as raw material. The remedy is wisdom, humility and moral reflection.”
ask: What are the Church’s key bioethics principles? (Dignity from conception; never use persons as means; procreation in marital act; ends don’t justify means.)
Which stem-cell sources are ethical? (Adult, cord blood, iPS cells; not embryonic.)
What question should we ask of new technology? (Should we, not only can we.)
practice: Choose three technologies: embryo screening, AI chat companions, organ transplant.
Apply five questions to each.
Decide what you think the Church would say and what guardrails are needed.
Write a rule you would adopt for your own use of technology.
script.close: Pray the prayer to St. Raphael for healing and guidance. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Discuss one bioethics question with a family member.”

tryit: Judge three technologies by the questions the Church asks.
Mark what serves persons.
Write a rule you would adopt.
lessons.saintStory:
Raphael is one of the three archangels named in Scripture, with Michael and Gabriel. His name in Hebrew means “God heals.” He appears in the Book of Tobit, in which an older man, Tobit, goes blind, and his son Tobias sets out on a long journey to collect a debt. Tobias hires a companion, who is really Raphael in disguise.
On the journey, a large fish leaps out of the river and tries to swallow Tobias. Raphael tells him to catch it, and to keep its heart, liver and gall, which are useful as medicine. In a distant city, they stay with Raguel, whose daughter Sarah has been widowed seven times because a demon killed each of her husbands on the wedding night. Raphael instructs Tobias how to drive away the demon, and Tobias and Sarah marry.
Back home, Raphael tells Tobias to put the fish’s gall on his father’s eyes, and Tobit regains his sight. Raphael then reveals himself: “I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter before the glory of the Lord.” “Bless God.” He is the patron of the sick, of physicians and travelers.

units.title: Other Churches and religions
units.eq: How does the Church relate to others?

lessons.title: Eastern Churches and the Orthodox
lessons.idea: The Orthodox Churches and the Eastern Catholic Churches are very close to the Catholic Church: they share apostolic succession, valid sacraments, the Creed and devotion to Mary and the saints. The main differences concern papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and some doctrines.
lessons.question: What are the differences?
lessons.activity: “Visit an Eastern church” (60 min). Attend a Divine Liturgy (or watch a recording). Students note: the iconostasis, incense, chant, the priest’s role, the epiclesis, communion with leavened bread. Afterwards they list what felt familiar and what was new, and write a note of thanks.
teach: The Eastern Churches possess true sacraments, especially the priesthood and Eucharist (CCC 838, 1399–1400; Unitatis Redintegratio 14–18). Catholics may receive Communion in Orthodox churches in some circumstances when no Catholic ministers are available, as the Code of Canon Law provides.
Differences: authority of the Pope, the Filioque, purgatory, the Immaculate Conception, divorce and remarriage.
Eastern Catholic Churches are in full communion with the Pope, with their own rites, canon law and married priests.
Pope John Paul II’s “two lungs” image and Ut Unum Sint call for continued dialogue.
talk: What do we share with the Orthodox?
quiz: The main differences between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches concern…|Papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque and some later doctrines|The existence of the sacraments|Baptism|The Creed’s first line|0|CCC 838; Unitatis Redintegratio 14–18.
An Eastern Catholic Church is…|A schismatic body|A Protestant group|A Church in full communion with Rome that keeps its own rite and discipline|An Orthodox Church|2|CCC 1203, 1399.

Why does the Catholic Church call the Orthodox Churches “sister Churches”?|They use Latin|They accept the Pope|They have true sacraments and apostolic succession|They share the same calendar|2|CCC 838, 1399.
lessons.saint: Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky: a Ukrainian Greek Catholic leader who hid Jews and kept the East’s traditions alive.
misc: “Orthodox and Catholics are totally different religions.”
“Reunion would require one side to surrender.”
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17. Ask: “What does Jesus pray for? How might the Churches heed that?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state three points of agreement and two of difference between Catholic and Orthodox.

script.open: Show an icon and a Western painting side by side. Ask, “What differences do you notice? What do you think they teach about how each tradition prays?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Eastern Christianity includes two groups. The Orthodox Churches, not in communion with the Pope, are about 260 million members: Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Georgian and others, led by patriarchs, with the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople as ‘first among equals.’ The Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac) separated after the Council of Chalcedon (451). The Eastern Catholic Churches: 23 Churches in communion with Rome with their own rites and laws, such as Ukrainian, Maronite, Melkite, Syro-Malabar, Chaldean, and Ruthenian. About 18 million Catholics. The Latin (Roman) Church is the largest, but one of many. All are fully Catholic. Vatican II’s Orientalium Ecclesiarum affirms their equal dignity.”

Say: “What the Orthodox and Catholics share: the Nicene Creed (except one word), seven sacraments, valid bishops and priests in apostolic succession, the Real Presence, devotion to Mary (the Theotokos), saints, icons, monasticism, the Fathers, and the first seven ecumenical councils. The main differences: the papacy (Orthodox accept the Pope as bishop of Rome with a primacy of honor, but reject universal jurisdiction and infallibility); the filioque (the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’), a Western addition; some other doctrines such as the Immaculate Conception, purgatory, and divorce and remarriage (Orthodox permit remarriage in certain cases). Style: the East emphasizes mystery, liturgy as heaven on earth, theosis (divinization), and icons; the West, systematic theology, law and activity.”

Say: “Eastern liturgy: the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, with chant, incense and the iconostasis; the sacraments of initiation given together to infants (Baptism, chrismation, Eucharist); married priests; leavened bread. Prayer: the Jesus Prayer, hesychasm. Relations: the Great Schism of 1054; the Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople in 1204; the failed unions of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439); the Union of Brest (1596). Contemporary: Paul VI and Athenagoras lifted the excommunications in 1965; John Paul II’s ‘two lungs’; the Joint Declaration with Patriarch Kirill (2016). Challenges: Ukraine, where Eastern Catholics and Orthodox have both suffered. The Church prays for full communion. What can Western Catholics do? Learn about the East, attend an Eastern liturgy, read the Eastern Fathers, and pray for unity.”
ask: How many Eastern Catholic Churches are there? (23.)
Name two differences between Orthodox and Catholic belief. (The papacy and the filioque.)
What is the iconostasis? (The icon screen separating the nave from the sanctuary in Eastern churches.)
practice: Make a Venn diagram of Orthodox / Catholic / shared.
Fill in at least eight items in the overlap.
Write three things you admire in the Eastern tradition.
Plan a visit to an Eastern church or reading of an Eastern author.
script.close: Pray the Trisagion: “Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn how the Divine Liturgy begins.”

tryit: Compare East and West on five points.
Mark what we share.
Describe Eastern Catholic Churches.
lessons.saintStory:
Roman Sheptytsky was born in 1865 into an old Ukrainian noble family in Galicia (now western Ukraine). He studied law and served in the Austrian army, then astonished his family by becoming a Basilian monk, taking the name Andrey. In 1901 he became metropolitan archbishop of Lviv for the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, which has an Eastern rite but is in communion with Rome. He led for forty-four years.
He founded schools, a national museum and a hospital, supported the poor with his own money, and promoted the Church’s Eastern heritage. He also longed for the union of the Eastern Churches with Rome, while respecting the Orthodox. In World War II, he opposed the Nazi occupation. He hid about 150 Jews, including children, in monasteries and in his own residence, and in 1942 wrote a pastoral letter, “Thou Shalt Not Kill,” condemning the murder of Jews. He wrote to Himmler, protesting.
He died in 1944. Pope Francis declared him Venerable in 2015. His life shows the Eastern Catholic Church in the 20th century: faithful in persecution, linking East and West.

lessons.title: Protestant communities
lessons.idea: Protestant communities share with Catholics Baptism, Scripture and faith in Christ, but differ on authority, the sacraments, ministry and justification. The Church speaks with respect and works for unity.
lessons.question: What do we share?
lessons.activity: “Study Unitatis Redintegratio” (45 min). Students read UR 19–24 and summarize what it says about Protestant communities: elements of truth, genuine Christian life, differences, and the invitation to dialogue. Compare the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) with Reformation-era disputes.
teach: Those who are baptized and believe in Christ are in a certain, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church (CCC 818–819). Their communities possess elements of sanctification and truth.
Differences: sola scriptura vs. Scripture and Tradition; papal authority; the Eucharist; Mary and the saints; seven sacraments vs. two or three.
Ecumenism includes prayer, theological dialogue, shared service. The Church recognizes Protestant Baptism if properly done with water and the Trinitarian formula (CCC 1256).
Avoid proselytizing; witness with charity and clarity.
quiz: What shared ground does the Church recognize with Protestant communities?|None|The papacy|The Mass|Baptism, Scripture and faith in Christ (CCC 818–819)|3|CCC 818–819.

The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification showed that Catholics and Lutherans…|Share a basic consensus on justification by grace through faith while some differences remain|Denied grace|Were in schism still|Agree on everything|0|Joint Declaration.
Which is a real Catholic–Protestant difference?|Belief in Jesus|Baptism with water|The authority of Scripture alone versus Scripture with Tradition and the Magisterium|Belief in God|2|CCC 80–82.
lessons.saint: Dietrich Bonhoeffer: a Lutheran pastor hanged by the Nazis, honored by Catholics among the martyrs of the twentieth century.
lessons.mem: “There is one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism.” (Ephesians 4:4–5)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 4:1–6. Ask: “What does Paul call us to?” Unity in one body.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain common ground with Protestants and two real differences.

script.open: Ask, “What do you know about Protestants? What do you admire about them? What do you find confusing?” Take answers, and note misconceptions.
teach: Say: “Protestant communities arose from the sixteenth-century Reformation. About 900 million people. Main families: Lutherans (from Martin Luther, in Germany and Scandinavia); Reformed and Presbyterian (from Calvin and Zwingli); Anglicans (the Church of England and Anglican Communion); Baptists; Methodists; Pentecostals and charismatics (the fastest-growing); and thousands of independent churches. They share belief in the Trinity, the divinity of Christ, the authority of Scripture, and salvation through Christ. Vatican II (Unitatis Redintegratio 3) says those who believe in Christ and are baptized are ‘in some, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church’ and have ‘a right to be called Christians’ and ‘are properly regarded as brothers and sisters in the Lord.’”

Say: “The Reformation principles: sola scriptura (Scripture alone), sola fide (faith alone), sola gratia (grace alone), the priesthood of all believers. Catholic response: Scripture is the inspired word of God, and also needs Tradition and the Church to be interpreted; faith and works are related; sacraments are real means of grace; the Church has a visible structure with bishops and the Pope. Differences: the number of sacraments (most Protestants recognize two, Baptism and the Lord’s Supper); the Eucharist (Lutherans hold a real presence; Reformed varied; many see it as symbolic); the papacy; Mary and the saints; the canon (Protestants omit the deuterocanonical books); clergy and celibacy; authority and Tradition; the Church’s visibility.”

Say: “Progress and cooperation. Official dialogues: Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration on Justification (1999); Anglican-Roman Catholic International Commission (ARCIC); with Methodists and Reformed. Shared witness: pro-life work, charity, Bible societies, hymns and prayer. Catholic respect for Protestants: gratitude for their devotion to Scripture, evangelistic zeal, and hymnody. Cautions: avoid indifferentism (‘it doesn’t matter what we believe’) and avoid proselytizing. Marriage: mixed marriages need permission; Communion: usually not shared across churches because it signifies full unity. Bonhoeffer’s story shows the shared witness of martyrdom. Tips for respectful conversation: listen first; ask what they believe, don’t assume; know your own faith; focus on common ground first; avoid caricatures; pray together; and remember that many have been hurt by division.”
ask: Name the four Reformation ‘solas’ listed. (Scripture, faith, grace, and the priesthood of all believers.)
What does the Church call baptized Protestants? (Brothers and sisters in the Lord, in imperfect communion.)
Why is Communion not shared across churches? (It signifies full unity of faith and communion.)
practice: Make a three-column chart: What we share / Where we differ / How to talk.
Fill in at least five items in each.
Prepare three good questions to ask a Protestant friend.
Plan an ecumenical action: shared service, prayer or Bible study.
script.close: Pray for Christian unity: “That they may all be one.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Invite a friend of another denomination to a shared service project.”

tryit: Compare Catholic and Protestant positions on five points.
State what we share.
Plan a respectful conversation.
lessons.saintStory:
Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born in 1906 in Breslau, Germany, into a family of scholars. He studied theology at Berlin and Union Theological Seminary in New York, where he attended the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem and was struck by its faith. He became a Lutheran pastor and teacher. When Hitler came to power in 1933, he opposed the Nazi interference in the church and helped found the Confessing Church. He led an underground seminary at Finkenwalde and wrote The Cost of Discipleship, arguing against “cheap grace.”
He could have stayed safe in the United States, but returned to Germany in 1939, saying he must share the trials of his people. He joined the resistance and helped Jews escape. He was arrested in April 1943. In prison, he wrote letters and poems, later published as Letters and Papers from Prison. He was implicated in a plot against Hitler.
He was hanged at Flossenbürg on April 9, 1945, just before the Allies arrived. His last words reportedly: “This is the end — for me the beginning of life.” John Paul II included him in the ecumenical commemoration of twentieth-century martyrs in 2000.

lessons.title: Judaism, Islam and other religions
lessons.idea: The Church honors the Jewish people as the people of the first covenant, esteems Muslims who worship the one God, and respects what is true and holy in other religions. She calls Catholics to dialogue and to reject all anti-Semitism and hatred.
lessons.question: How do we dialogue?
lessons.activity: “Interreligious conversation” (60 min). Invite guests or visit a synagogue, mosque, or other house of worship. Prepare respectful questions. Afterward reflect: what did we share? What distinguishes our faith? How can we cooperate for good?
teach: The Church recognizes the Jewish people as God’s first-called people. “To them belong the sonship, the glory, the covenants” (Romans 9:4). Anti-Semitism is a sin against the Gospel (CCC 839–840; Nostra Aetate 4).
Muslims profess the faith of Abraham and worship the one merciful God. We share much, though we differ about Christ and the Trinity (CCC 841).
Other religions contain rays of truth (CCC 843–845). The Church’s mission remains to proclaim Christ, with respect for freedom.
Catholic–Jewish and Catholic–Muslim dialogues continue.
talk: What do we share with Jews?
quiz: Nostra Aetate teaches that the Jewish people…|Must be avoided|Remain beloved of God, whose gifts and call are irrevocable (Romans 11:29)|Are collectively guilty|Have been replaced by the Church|1|CCC 839–840.

Which sentence best captures the Church’s view of other religions?|They are to be ignored|All are equal|They contain nothing true|The Church rejects nothing true and holy in them, and still proclaims Christ|3|CCC 843; NA 2.
Interreligious dialogue, for the Church, is…|A part of mission that listens and bears witness with respect|Only for experts|Forbidden|A replacement for mission|0|CCC 856.
lessons.saint: Blessed Christian de Chergé and the monks of Tibhirine: seven French monks who stayed in Algeria among Muslim neighbors, and were killed in 1996.
lessons.mem: “For the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.” (Romans 11:29)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 11:1–2, 11:29. Ask: “What does Paul say about God’s gifts to Israel?” “Irrevocable.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Church’s attitude toward Jews, Muslims and other religions.

script.open: Draw a circle and label it ‘my faith.’ Ask students to add smaller circles around it for people they know of other faiths or none. Have each student name one thing they admire about someone in a circle.
teach: Say: “Nostra Aetate (1965) is the Church’s declaration on relations with non-Christian religions. It affirms: ‘The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions. She regards with sincere reverence those ways of conduct and of life, those precepts and teachings which, though differing in many particulars from what she holds and sets forth, nonetheless often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all men.’ At the same time, the Church ‘proclaims, and is duty bound to proclaim without fail, Christ who is ‘the way, the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6).’ Dialogue doesn’t mean giving up conviction, but listening and respecting.”

Say: “Judaism: the Church’s elder brother. Christianity is rooted in Israel. The Old Testament is our Scripture. Jesus, Mary and the apostles were Jews. The Church condemns antisemitism and holds that the Jewish people are not guilty of Jesus’ death, and that God’s covenant with them is irrevocable (Romans 11:29). John Paul II called Jews ‘our dearly beloved brothers’ and ‘our elder brothers.’ Differences: Jews do not accept Jesus as Messiah. Islam: Muslims worship the one God, merciful and almighty, creator of heaven and earth. They honor Jesus as a prophet (not God), revere Mary, and fast and give alms. Differences: Trinity, Incarnation, Jesus’ crucifixion, the authority of the Qur’an and Muhammad. The Council urged mutual understanding. Hinduism and Buddhism: they seek answers to the great questions; the Church encourages respect and sees ‘seeds of the Word.’”

Say: “Principles. One: human dignity and religious freedom. Two: truth is found wherever it is, but fullness in Christ. Three: the Church’s mission remains, but evangelization respects freedom and is done in love and example. Four: cooperation on shared goods: peace, poverty, life, family. The Assisi gathering (1986). The 2019 Document on Human Fraternity. Practical: learn about neighbors’ faith from them; visit a mosque or synagogue; welcome neighbors; avoid stereotypes; speak honestly about differences; do not syncretize (mixing). The Tibhirine monks lived dialogue in daily friendship. Dialogue of life, action, theological exchange and spiritual experience. Our own faith deepens when we meet others with openness and clarity.”
ask: What does Nostra Aetate say about other religions? (The Church rejects nothing true and holy in them.)
What is the Church’s view of Jews today? (Elder brothers; the covenant is irrevocable; antisemitism is condemned.)
What do Muslims share with Christians? (Worship of one God, honor for Jesus as prophet and Mary.)
practice: Make a table: Judaism / Islam / Hinduism / Buddhism: shared beliefs, key differences, one respectful practice.
Write three rules for interfaith friendship.
Choose one neighbor or classmate of another faith and plan a friendly conversation.
Write a prayer for peace among the faiths.
script.close: Pray for peace among believers. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Have a respectful conversation with someone of another faith.”

tryit: Describe what we share with Judaism and Islam.
Describe where we differ.
Write a rule for interfaith friendship.
lessons.saintStory:
In the 1990s, a civil war raged in Algeria between the government and Islamist militants. At the Trappist monastery of Our Lady of the Atlas in Tibhirine, in the mountains, nine monks lived and prayed among their Muslim neighbors, running a small clinic and farm. The prior, Christian de Chergé, had been an army officer in Algeria in the 1950s, where an Algerian friend, a Muslim named Mohammed, saved his life, and later died protecting him. That deep friendship shaped his vocation.
When the threats grew, the monks were told to leave. They voted to stay, out of solidarity with the villagers. On the night of March 26-27, 1996, armed men kidnapped seven monks. Two months later they were found dead.
Christian de Chergé had written a testament, to be opened in the event of his death. He wrote that he forgave in advance his killer, “my last-minute friend,” and prayed that they would meet in paradise “like happy good thieves.” He was beatified in 2018 with eighteen other martyrs of Algeria. The Muslims of Tibhirine mourned them.

units.title: Apologetics: giving a reason
units.eq: Why do Catholics believe what they believe?

lessons.title: Scripture and authority
lessons.idea: Sola scriptura (“Scripture alone”) is the claim that the Bible is the sole authority. Catholics respond with Scripture and history: Scripture itself points to Tradition and the Church, the canon was set by the Church, and a pillar of truth is needed to settle disputes.
lessons.question: How do we respond?
lessons.activity: “Use the Apologetics section” (45 min). Students use the Apologetics section of the app. For each of three objections (“sola scriptura is biblical”, “traditions of men”, “Catholic traditions contradict the Bible”), they gather verses (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 3:15; 2 Peter 1:20; Matthew 15:3–9) and historical facts (the canon) and write a concise reply.
teach: Scripture and Tradition together form the deposit of faith (CCC 80–82). 2 Thessalonians 2:15 commends oral and written traditions. 1 Timothy 3:15 calls the Church “the pillar and bulwark of the truth.”
2 Timothy 3:16–17 says Scripture is “profitable,” not that it is “sufficient alone.” The canon itself was determined by the Church’s Tradition.
Jesus condemned human traditions that contradict God’s commands (Mark 7:8), not apostolic tradition.
Be fair: Protestants hold to the high authority of Scripture and many regard creeds and confessions as authoritative. Dialogue calmly.
talk: How do you respond to sola scriptura?
quiz: Which is the strongest reply to “the Bible alone is our authority”?|Tradition replaces Scripture|The canon itself was recognized by the Church, and the New Testament points to oral tradition and to the Church as the pillar of truth|Scripture is unimportant|The Bible is false|1|2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Timothy 3:15.

2 Timothy 3:16–17 says Scripture is “profitable.” A careful reply notes that it…|Says Scripture alone suffices|Denies Scripture|Does not claim Scripture alone is sufficient, only useful|Applies only to the New Testament|2|Profitable does not mean sufficient alone.
The Catholic view of Tradition is that it…|Is only written|Is the living transmission of the Gospel, not a second source that contradicts Scripture|Is optional custom|Adds new revelation|1|CCC 80–82.
lessons.saint: Edmund Campion: a brilliant Oxford scholar who came secretly to England to argue for the faith and died for it.
lessons.mem: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.” (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Where does the Bible say ‘the Bible alone’?” Open 2 Timothy 3:16 and read carefully. Ask what it says and does not say.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give a concise reply to sola scriptura with two Scriptural and one historical point.

script.open: Write the line ‘Where does the Bible say that?’ on the board. Ask a student to play a skeptical friend who says it, and let two volunteers try an answer in thirty seconds each. Debrief on what worked.
teach: Say: “Apologetics means giving reasons for faith. 1 Peter 3:15: ‘Always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who calls you to account for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and reverence.’ Tone matters. First, listen: understand what the person actually believes. Second, find common ground. Third, respond with reasons, clearly. Fourth, be humble. The goal is to win the person, not the argument. Many objections come from misunderstandings of Catholic teaching, or from real wounds. Apologetics clears the way; the Holy Spirit converts.”

Say: “Sola scriptura: the claim that the Bible alone is the authority. Catholic reply. One: the Bible does not say it. 2 Timothy 3:16 says Scripture is ‘profitable’ but doesn’t say ‘only.’ Two: the Bible itself points to Tradition (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 2 Timothy 2:2; John 21:25) and to the Church as ‘the pillar and bulwark of the truth’ (1 Timothy 3:15). Three: the New Testament canon was determined by the Church. Four: the Bible requires interpretation; Protestants disagree widely, resulting in tens of thousands of denominations. Five: the early Church had no Bible as we know it for decades, and was guided by apostolic teaching. Six: Jesus established a Church with authority (Matthew 16, 18). This isn’t against Scripture but about how Scripture is read. Catholics honor Scripture: they read it at every Mass.”

Say: “Other common questions on Scripture and authority. ‘Why do Catholics have extra books?’ The Septuagint, used by Jesus’ contemporaries, included them; Luther’s removal followed a later Jewish canon. ‘Why do you call priests Father?’ Jesus’ warning (Matthew 23:9) is against pride; Paul calls himself spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15). ‘Is the Pope in the Bible?’ Matthew 16:18-19; John 21:15-17; Luke 22:32. ‘What about tradition of men?’ Mark 7:8 condemns human traditions that contradict God’s word, not apostolic Tradition. Method: use the Bible and history, and always charity. Campion’s approach was clear and respectful, and he stayed calm in the face of death. The witness of life is the strongest apologetic.”
ask: What does apologetics mean? (Giving reasons for faith.)
What does 1 Peter 3:15 say about tone? (With gentleness and reverence.)
Give one Catholic reply to sola scriptura. (The Bible doesn’t teach it; the Church determined the canon; Tradition is in Scripture.)
practice: Choose three common objections and write a short, courteous reply with Scripture for each.
Practice with a partner: one asks, the other answers in 60 seconds.
Evaluate: Did the answer listen first? Was it charitable?
Write one question you want to find an answer to.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me the right words and a gentle heart.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn one good Scripture argument well.”

tryit: Answer “Where does the Bible say that?” with three sources.
Build a short argument for the Church’s role.
Write the reply to sola scriptura.
lessons.saintStory:
Edmund Campion was born in London in 1540, and became a star at Oxford. Queen Elizabeth I visited the university in 1566, and Campion, then a young scholar, delivered a speech in front of her. He was ordained an Anglican deacon, but became troubled by doubts. By 1571, he was convinced of the Catholic faith and fled to Douai, in France, where he was received back. He joined the Jesuits in 1573.
In 1580, he returned secretly to England, which was then dangerous for priests: it was treason to be a Catholic priest. Disguised as a jewel merchant, he traveled the country, saying Mass and hearing confessions. He wrote a letter of challenge to the Privy Council, “Campion’s Brag,” offering to debate any scholar, and wrote a book, Ten Reasons (Rationes Decem), defending the faith by arguments from Scripture and history. It was printed secretly and left on the benches of Oxford’s church.
He was caught in July 1581, tortured, and forced to debate in the Tower. In December, he was condemned and hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn, on December 1, 1581. He was canonized in 1970 among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

lessons.title: The Eucharist and the saints
lessons.idea: The Real Presence and the intercession of the saints are two doctrines often challenged. The biblical and patristic evidence for them is strong: John 6, the words of institution, 1 Corinthians 10–11, and the early Church’s practice of honoring martyrs.
lessons.question: What is your best argument?
lessons.activity: “Practice” (45 min). Pairs role-play a friendly conversation: one raises an objection (“Isn’t communion just a symbol?”; “Why pray to saints?”), the other responds with Scripture (John 6:53–56; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29; Revelation 5:8) and Fathers (Ignatius, Justin, Cyril of Jerusalem). Switch roles and give feedback on tone.
teach: The Church believes in the Real Presence on the basis of Christ’s words and the unanimous witness of the early Church (CCC 1374–1376). Ignatius (c. 107): “the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.”
The saints intercede for us (CCC 956–957; Revelation 5:8, 6:9–10). The early Church honored martyrs’ tombs and asked for their prayers (catacomb inscriptions).
Avoid proof-texting. Show the whole pattern of Scripture and Tradition.
Always remember the person: a good answer is gentle and patient.
talk: How do you respond to objections?
quiz: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107) matters for the Real Presence because he…|Wrote after the Reformation|Called the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ”|Denied it|Never mentioned it|1|Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7.

A Protestant friend says asking saints to pray is idolatry. A good Catholic answer begins by…|Avoiding Scripture|Quoting only Mary|Distinguishing worship due to God alone from asking fellow members of Christ’s body to pray for us (CCC 956–957, 2683)|Dismissing the objection|2|Veneration is not adoration.
Which verse supports the saints’ intercession by showing heavenly beings offering prayers?|Psalm 23|Genesis 1:1|Revelation 5:8|Romans 3:23|2|Revelation 5:8; 6:9–10.
lessons.saint: Venerable Fulton Sheen: an archbishop who explained the faith to millions on television and prayed an hour before the Eucharist every day.
misc: “Early Christians saw the Eucharist as a symbol.”
lessons.mem: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.” (John 6:53)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you were to prove to a skeptic that Christians have always believed in the Real Presence, what would you show?” List the sources.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a two-minute answer to an objection about the Eucharist or saints.

script.open: Ask, “A friend says, ‘You think a piece of bread is God, and you pray to dead people. Isn’t that weird?’ How would you answer without getting defensive?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “On the Eucharist. Objection: ‘It’s only a symbol.’ Reply: John 6. Jesus says, ‘My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.’ (6:55) He uses a strong verb for ‘eat’ (trogein, ‘gnaw’). When many disciples left, he did not say, ‘You misunderstood, I was speaking symbolically.’ He let them go. At the Last Supper he said, ‘This is my body,’ not ‘This represents.’ Paul: those who receive unworthily are ‘guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.’ (1 Corinthians 11:27) The early Church: Ignatius of Antioch (AD 107) said heretics ‘abstain from the Eucharist because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.’ Justin Martyr (AD 155): it is not common bread. No Christian writer for a thousand years taught that it was merely a symbol.”

Say: “On the saints. Objection: ‘Praying to saints takes away from Jesus; Scripture says there’s one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).’ Reply: We ask saints for prayers, as we ask each other. Paul asked for prayers (Romans 15:30). If it’s fine to ask a friend on earth to pray, why not one in heaven? The dead in Christ are alive: ‘He is not God of the dead, but of the living.’ (Matthew 22:32) Revelation 5:8 and 6:9-10 shows saints in heaven offering prayers and interceding. Hebrews 12:1: ‘a cloud of witnesses.’ We don’t worship saints; we honor them. We do not take away from Christ; the saints are his members. On Mary: Luke 1:48, ‘All generations will call me blessed.’ On statues: not idols but reminders, as photographs.”

Say: “Other common objections. ‘Why confess to a priest?’ John 20:23. ‘Why call the Eucharist a sacrifice?’ Malachi 1:11; Hebrews 13:10; 1 Corinthians 10:16-18. ‘Mass is boring repetition.’ Matthew 6:7 condemns empty babbling, not prayer; the Mass is rich in Scripture. Tone: Sheen said, ‘Hate the error, love the person who holds it.’ Be willing to say ‘I don’t know, I’ll find out.’ Use the Catechism and good resources. Pray before a conversation. After the conversation, pray for the person. Best apologetic: a life of joy, charity and integrity, and an invitation to ‘come and see’ (John 1:46). Sheen’s holy hour was the secret behind his preaching.”
ask: What does John 6 teach? (Jesus’ flesh and blood are real food and drink.)
Why do Catholics ask saints to pray? (Same reason we ask friends; they are alive in Christ.)
What was Sheen’s daily practice? (A holy hour before the Blessed Sacrament.)
practice: Pair up. One plays the skeptic, one the Catholic, using the Eucharist or saints objection.
The Catholic must listen, affirm common ground, give a Scripture reason, and invite a conversation.
Swap roles.
Debrief: what worked, what felt defensive?
script.close: Pray quietly before the Blessed Sacrament if possible, or: “Jesus, I adore you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make a holy hour or a half-hour of adoration this month.”

tryit: Answer an objection about the Eucharist using John 6 and the Fathers.
Answer an objection about praying to saints.
Evaluate the tone.
lessons.saintStory:
Fulton Sheen was born in 1895 in Illinois, and was ordained a priest in 1919. He earned a doctorate in philosophy in Belgium, was a professor at Catholic University, and a gifted preacher. He promised at ordination to spend a holy hour daily before the Blessed Sacrament, and did so for the next sixty years.
In 1951 he began a TV program, Life Is Worth Living. Wearing a cape, standing in front of a blackboard with no script, he spoke about faith, culture, family and communism in clear language. Tens of millions watched; he won an Emmy in 1952. He was consecrated bishop in 1951, and directed the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, giving away the money from his broadcasts to the missions. He later became bishop of Rochester, New York, and an archbishop.
He converted many through his talks, including notable figures. He died in 1979. He was declared Venerable in 2012. He said, “There are not one hundred people in America who hate the Catholic Church, but there are millions who hate what they wrongly think the Catholic Church is.”

lessons.title: Confession and the papacy
lessons.idea: Two common objections concern Confession (“Why go to a priest?”) and the papacy (“Why is Peter the rock?”). John 20:21–23 and Matthew 16:13–19 are central, and the early Church’s practice supports the Catholic understanding.
lessons.question: How do we respond with charity?
lessons.activity: “Role-play” (45 min). In trios (questioner, responder, observer), students practice answering: “Only God can forgive sins” and “Peter is just a pebble (petros) not the rock (petra).” Use Mark 2:7–10, John 20:23, the Aramaic “Kepha,” Isaiah 22:22, and early testimonies (Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Cyprian). Observers give feedback.
teach: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins in his name (John 20:21–23; CCC 1441–1442). “God has reconciled us to himself and given us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).
The papacy: Peter is the rock (Matthew 16:18), receives the keys (Isaiah 22:22; Matthew 16:19), confirms his brothers (Luke 22:32) and feeds the flock (John 21:15–17) (CCC 881–882).
In Aramaic Jesus said “Kepha” for both Peter and the rock. Early Fathers acknowledge Rome’s special authority (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3).
Present the doctrine of papal infallibility accurately (see earlier grades).
talk: How do we answer with charity?
quiz: In John 20:21–23, Jesus…|Tells the apostles to avoid sin|Gives the apostles the power to forgive and retain sins|Appoints a single scribe|Forbids confession|1|CCC 1441–1442.

The Aramaic “Kepha” in Matthew 16:18 helps answer the claim that Peter is just a “pebble” because…|It is not mentioned|It means pebble|Jesus likely used the same word for Peter and the rock|It is Greek|2|The Greek petros and petra reflect the Aramaic kepha.

Which best describes papal infallibility?|The Pope is sinless|The Pope, teaching definitively on faith or morals to the whole Church, is preserved from error (CCC 891)|Whatever he says is infallible|It applies to politics|1|CCC 891.
lessons.life: Practice explaining the papacy in 2 minutes.
lessons.saint: Callistus I: a former slave and convict who became pope and taught that the Church can forgive.
misc: “The priest forgives by his own authority.”
lessons.mem: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them.” (John 20:22–23)
lessons.hook: Read John 20:21–23 and Matthew 16:18–19. Ask: “What power does Jesus give? To whom?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to answer one objection about Confession and one about the papacy.

script.open: Set two chairs facing each other. Say, “One person is a Protestant friend asking about Confession; the other is you.” Choose two volunteers to act it for two minutes, then let the class give feedback.
teach: Say: “Confession. Objections: ‘Only God can forgive sins.’ Reply: True; and God has given the power to the apostles. John 20:21-23: ‘As the Father has sent me, even so I send you… If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven.’ Matthew 18:18: binding and loosing. 2 Corinthians 5:18: ‘God… gave us the ministry of reconciliation.’ James 5:16: ‘confess your sins to one another.’ Mark 2:7-10: Jesus forgave sins, and Matthew 9:8 says God gave such authority ‘to men.’ How would the apostles know whether to forgive or retain sins unless they heard them? The early Church practiced confession (Didache; Tertullian; Cyprian; Origen). Callistus’s assertion. The benefit: certainty of forgiveness, counsel, healing, and the support of the Church.”

Say: “The papacy. Objections: ‘Peter was a man, not a pope’; ‘the rock is Peter’s faith’; ‘the Pope is not in the Bible.’ Replies. Matthew 16:18-19: Jesus gives Simon a new name, Rock, and the keys, which in Isaiah 22:22 represent the office of the master of the household, who ‘shall open, and none shall shut.’ Peter is always first in lists of apostles (Matthew 10:2), speaks first at Pentecost, leads at the Council of Jerusalem, and Jesus prays for him in Luke 22:32 and commands him in John 21:15-17. The early Church recognized Rome’s primacy: Clement of Rome intervened in Corinth (AD 96); Ignatius wrote of Rome ‘presiding in love’; Irenaeus (AD 180) said all churches must agree with Rome ‘on account of its preeminent authority.’ Succession lists of popes go back to Peter. The Pope is the Vicar of Christ and servant of the servants of God.”

Say: “Objections to the papacy: bad popes in history (the Church admits sins; Judas was an apostle); infallibility (limited to definitions on faith and morals); Eastern Christians disagree about jurisdiction; the Reformation. Reply: Jesus promised that the gates of hell will not prevail; the papacy is a gift of unity. Unity needs a visible center, as nations need a constitution. A balanced presentation: the Pope is a successor of Peter, with real authority but under the word of God. Papal primacy is not meant to crush the bishops’ role but to serve unity. Pope Francis’s emphasis on the Pope as pastor and servant. We pray for the Pope at every Mass. Callistus reminds us that the Church includes sinners, and the Church’s power to forgive is part of its mission.”
ask: What Scripture shows Jesus gave the apostles authority to forgive sins? (John 20:21-23.)
What do the keys of Matthew 16 recall? (The steward’s office in Isaiah 22.)
Which early witnesses affirm Rome’s primacy? (Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus.)
practice: Make two argument maps: Confession and the papacy, each with Scripture, early Church and reason.
List the two strongest objections and replies for each.
Practice a 90-second summary of one argument.
Evaluate each other’s tone.
script.close: Pray for the Pope and the Church’s leaders. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Matthew 16:13-20 and John 20:19-23 slowly.”

tryit: Build a case for Peter’s role from three texts.
Build a case for priestly absolution.
Prepare replies to two objections.
lessons.saintStory:
Callistus was born a slave in Rome in the second century. His master, Carpophorus, a Christian, gave him money to set up a bank for Christian widows and others. The bank failed, and Callistus fled but was caught. Some accounts say he was beaten and sent to a treadmill; later he was sentenced to the mines of Sardinia for a disturbance. He was freed through the intervention of a Christian woman close to the emperor’s household.
Pope Zephyrinus made him a deacon in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way, which is still called the Catacombs of Callistus. He became bishop of Rome in about 217. He taught that the Church could forgive even grave sins like adultery after penance, which scandalized rigorists such as Hippolytus, who thought it was too lax. Callistus held that the Church is not a society of the perfect but includes the wheat and the weeds together.
He was martyred around 222, tradition says thrown from a window in Trastevere. His pontificate marks an early assertion of the Church’s power to forgive.

lessons.title: Death and judgment
lessons.idea: Death ends our earthly pilgrimage. Each person is judged by Christ immediately after death (particular judgment) and again at the end of time (general judgment). Hebrews 9:27: “It is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment.” This is a call to live now with love.
lessons.question: How should we prepare?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (40 min). Students write a reflective piece on the Church’s teaching on death and judgment, ending with a short examination of conscience and a list of what matters most. Offer silent prayer and, if desired, the Prayer for a Happy Death.
teach: Death is the end of earthly life and the entrance to eternal life (CCC 1005–1014). Christ transformed death: for believers, it is a participation in his death and resurrection (CCC 1006–1009).
The particular judgment: “Each man receives his eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of his death” (CCC 1022). The general judgment will reveal all (CCC 1038–1041).
We are judged on love (Matthew 25). Mercy and justice meet in Christ (CCC 679).
Remember to speak gently with students who have lost loved ones. Memento mori is spiritual practice, not morbid fear.
quiz: Hebrews 9:27 (“appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment”) is used to rule out…|The resurrection|Prayer|Reincarnation|Heaven|2|CCC 1013.
The particular judgment happens…|Only for saints|Never|At the end of time|Immediately after death, when each soul receives its eternal destiny (CCC 1022)|3|CCC 1022.
What will the general judgment reveal?|Only the sins of the wicked|Nothing new|Only Church history|The full meaning of history and of God’s justice and mercy (CCC 1040)|3|CCC 1038–1041.
lessons.life: Write a letter to your future self about eternity.
lessons.saint: Joseph: tradition says he died with Jesus and Mary at his side, which is why he is patron of a happy death.
lessons.mem: “It is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment.” (Hebrews 9:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you had one year to live, what would change?” Take answers. Then read Hebrews 9:27.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the particular and general judgment and how they shape life now.

script.open: Place a blank sheet and a pen at the center and say, “Write your own obituary in three lines, what you would most want said of you.” Allow three minutes of quiet writing. Collect a few to read, with permission.
teach: Say: “The Catechism teaches what the Church calls the ‘last things’ or eschatology: death, judgment, heaven, hell, and the end of the world. Death: the separation of the soul from the body. The body decays, the soul, which is immortal, goes to meet God. Death is a consequence of the fall (Romans 5:12), but Christ transformed it. ‘Our Savior Jesus Christ… abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.’ (2 Timothy 1:10) For the Christian, death is a passage. St. Paul: ‘For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.’ (Philippians 1:21) Death ends the time of merit; we have only one life (Hebrews 9:27: ‘It is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment’). So the Church rejects reincarnation.”

Say: “Judgment. The particular judgment: immediately at death, each soul receives its eternal retribution according to its faith and works (CCC 1021-1022). Luke 16 (Lazarus and the rich man), Luke 23:43 (the good thief: ‘today you will be with me in Paradise’). The destination: heaven (immediately or after purification), or hell. The general (final) judgment: at the end of time, Christ will come in glory, the dead will rise, and the whole truth of each life will be revealed. Matthew 25:31-46. The standard: love; ‘I was hungry and you gave me food.’ We will be judged on deeds of mercy. Also on faith (John 3:18). Judgment is a revelation of the truth and an act of justice and mercy.”

Say: “How should we live in light of this? The Church has a tradition of the memento mori: remembering death. Psalm 90:12: ‘So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.’ Not morbidly, but to focus on what matters. Practical: live in the state of grace; go to Confession regularly; receive the Eucharist; do works of mercy; forgive; make a will; tell loved ones you love them; and pray for a happy death, the Hail Mary: ‘now and at the hour of our death.’ The Church has rites for the dying: Anointing, Viaticum, Commendation. A happy death is a gift: St. Joseph is invoked. The particular and general judgment express that our choices matter. Fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, but ‘perfect love casts out fear’ (1 John 4:18).”
ask: What is the particular judgment? (Each soul’s judgment at death.)
What is the general judgment? (At the end of time, when Christ returns.)
Why does the Church reject reincarnation? (We die once, and then comes judgment.)
practice: Draw a line from birth to death, and mark what matters most: relationships, faith, service.
Write a list of five things you would want to have done by the end of your life.
Choose one to begin this month.
Write a short act of trust: “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit.”
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary slowly, especially the final line. Add: “St. Joseph, patron of a happy death, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a happy death daily.”

tryit: Explain death, particular judgment and general judgment.
Make a list of what you would want to have done.
Write a short act of trust.
lessons.saintStory:
The Gospels do not tell us how Joseph died. He is last seen when Jesus is twelve, in the Temple. By the time Jesus begins his public ministry, Joseph is no longer mentioned, and Mary is called a widow in later Christian tradition. Early Christian writings, such as the apocryphal History of Joseph the Carpenter, describe his death in old age, with Jesus and Mary beside him, comforting him.
That picture, whether a pious story or a deep intuition, shaped how the Church thinks of Joseph. Christians have long prayed to him for a happy death: a death in the state of grace, comforted by the sacraments, with Jesus and Mary near. Many churches have an altar to Joseph, and confraternities of the “happy death” were formed.
Joseph’s whole life was a preparation: he listened to God’s messengers in dreams, took Mary home, protected Jesus in danger, worked with his hands, and said nothing in the Gospels. The Church asks us to live as he did, so that we may die as he did.

lessons.title: Heaven, hell and purgatory
lessons.idea: After death, those who die in God’s grace and friendship and are perfectly purified live forever with him (heaven). Those who die in God’s friendship but need purification undergo purgatory. Those who freely and finally refuse him choose hell. The Church knows these as realities, not as maps.
lessons.question: What is purgatory?
lessons.activity: “Study” (45 min). Students read CCC 1023–1037 and compose a three-column summary: heaven (vision of God, communion), purgatory (purification, prayer for the dead, 2 Maccabees 12:45), hell (self-exclusion, the reality of freedom). Add a pastoral reflection on how the Church prays for the dead.
teach: Heaven is “the ultimate end and fulfillment of the deepest human longings” (CCC 1024). The blessed see God face to face (CCC 1023–1029).
Purgatory is a final purification (CCC 1030–1032). The Church prays for the dead and offers Masses, alms and indulgences for them.
Hell is a state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033–1037). God predestines no one to hell. The Church canonizes saints but never declares anyone damned.
Rather than speculation, the Church stresses hope and conversion.
quiz: Purgatory, according to the Church, is…|A second chance after death for those who rejected God|A place of eternal punishment|A final purification for those who die in God’s friendship but still need holiness (CCC 1030–1031)|A myth|2|CCC 1030–1032.

Hell is described in the Catechism as…|A place that must be earthly|The state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033)|A natural disaster|God’s decision to punish|1|CCC 1033, 1037.

Why do Catholics pray for the dead?|To change God’s mind|Because the Church on earth can help those being purified (2 Maccabees 12:45; CCC 1032)|Because it is required for salvation|To be superstitious|1|CCC 1032.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Genoa: a married laywoman who wrote that purgatory is the fire of love.
misc: “Purgatory is a second chance after death.”
lessons.mem: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him.” (1 Corinthians 2:9)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 16:19–31, the rich man and Lazarus. Ask: “What does the story warn about? What does it show about ongoing relationship?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain heaven, purgatory and hell and their pastoral implications.

script.open: Write three words on the board: Heaven, Purgatory, Hell. Ask, “Which of these do people today find hardest to believe? Why?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Heaven. The Catechism: ‘Those who die in God’s grace and friendship and are perfectly purified live for ever with Christ. They are like God for ever, for they ‘see him as he is’, face to face.’ (CCC 1023) This is the beatific vision: seeing God directly. 1 Corinthians 13:12: ‘Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face.’ Revelation 21:4: ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’ Heaven is communion with the Trinity, Mary, the angels and saints; fulfillment of every good desire; not boredom but joy beyond imagination: ‘What no eye has seen, nor ear heard… God has prepared for those who love him.’ (1 Corinthians 2:9) It includes the resurrection of the body at the end. The saints in heaven pray for us.”

Say: “Purgatory (see Grade 11). Catherine of Genoa taught that it’s not primarily a place of punishment but a process of purification by God’s love. The souls there are certain of heaven and joyful, but suffer from the delay. They can’t help themselves; we can help them by prayer and sacrifice. Hell. The Catechism: ‘To die in mortal sin without repenting and accepting God’s merciful love means remaining separated from him for ever by our own free choice. This state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God and the blessed is called ‘hell.’’ (CCC 1033) Hell is a real possibility (Matthew 25:41, 46; Mark 9:43-48). The Church teaches that God does not predestine anyone to hell; a person chooses it by rejecting love until the end. The main pain is the loss of God.”

Say: “Questions. ‘How could a loving God send people to hell?’ He doesn’t send; we choose. C. S. Lewis: ‘The doors of hell are locked on the inside.’ ‘Is anyone in hell?’ The Church has never declared that any person is in hell, not even Judas, but warns it is possible. The Church canonizes saints but not the damned. ‘Is hell eternal?’ Yes, the Church teaches that its punishment is eternal (CCC 1035). ‘What about those who never heard of Christ?’ God’s mercy can reach them (see Grade 10). Apparitions at Fatima describe a vision of hell, as a call to prayer. Our response is to take it seriously, to pray for sinners, and to trust in God’s mercy. Pope Benedict XVI’s Spe Salvi (45-47) says that in most people ‘there remains in the depths of their being an ultimate interior openness to truth, to love, to God,’ and that purification is needed on the way to him.”
ask: What is the beatific vision? (Seeing God face to face.)
What is hell, according to the Catechism? (Definitive self-exclusion from communion with God.)
Has the Church declared anyone to be in hell? (No.)
practice: Make a three-column chart: Heaven / Purgatory / Hell with key texts, definition, and common misconceptions.
Write a response to someone who says ‘a loving God wouldn’t allow hell.’
List what we can do for the souls in purgatory.
Compose a short prayer for the dead.
script.close: Pray: “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Offer a Mass or a decade for the souls in purgatory.”

tryit: Compare heaven, purgatory and hell.
Match each to Scripture and the Catechism.
State what the Church leaves undefined.
lessons.saintStory:
Caterina Fieschi was born in 1447 in Genoa, Italy, to a noble family. She wanted to enter a convent, but at sixteen, for political reasons, her family arranged her marriage to Giuliano Adorno, a wild young nobleman who was unfaithful and wasted her dowry on gambling and debt. For about ten years, she was miserable, and turned to worldly amusements.
On March 20, 1473, she went to confession in a church and was suddenly overwhelmed by a deep sense of God’s love and of her own sinfulness. She cried, “No more world! No more sin!” From then on, she devoted herself to prayer and service. She and Giuliano, who also changed, agreed to live as brother and sister, and both served the sick at the Pammatone Hospital in Genoa. When plague struck in 1493, she nursed the victims and nearly died herself.
Her spiritual writings, particularly her Treatise on Purgatory, describe the soul after death as drawn irresistibly to God, and yet ashamed, so that it wants to be purified by love. She died in 1510.

lessons.title: The new creation
lessons.idea: Scripture ends with the promise of new heavens and a new earth where God dwells with his people. Creation will be transformed and the body will rise. Christian hope is not escape from the world but its renewal.
lessons.question: What is the hope?
lessons.activity: “Meditation” (40 min). Students pray Revelation 21 slowly, imagining the scene. They list images and connect each to Genesis (tree of life, river). They write a short prayer of hope and reflect on how this vision affects work for justice and care for creation now.
teach: At the end the universe will be renewed: “a new heaven and a new earth” (CCC 1042–1050; Revelation 21:1). Our bodies will rise glorified (CCC 988–1004).
The vision of God, communion of saints and life with the Trinity are the fulfilment of human desire (CCC 1023–1029).
Christian hope motivates work in the world: “earthly progress must be carefully distinguished from the growth of Christ’s kingdom” yet it can contribute (CCC 1049).
The liturgy anticipates it: the Mass joins heaven and earth.
quiz: Christian hope for the “new heavens and new earth” implies that…|Creation will be renewed and transformed (CCC 1042–1050)|Matter is evil|Time will repeat|Creation will be destroyed|0|CCC 1042–1050.

The resurrection of the body means…|The body is lost forever|The soul alone survives|The whole person, glorified, will be raised, as Christ was (CCC 988–1004)|People return as new animals|2|CCC 988–1004.

Which attitude toward work and justice follows from this hope?|Fear|Effort to build up the world now, since earthly progress can serve the Kingdom without being identical with it (CCC 1049)|Indifference|Withdrawal from the world|1|CCC 1049.
lessons.saint: Gregory of Nyssa: a bishop who taught that heaven is endless growth into God.
misc: “The material world will be destroyed and forgotten.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)
lessons.hook: Read Revelation 21:1–5. Ask: “What is new? What is missing?” The story ends with a city and a garden.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the new creation and how it influences present action.

script.open: Ask, “Do you imagine heaven as endless sitting on clouds? What would make it truly a place of joy?” Take answers. “The Church has a much richer picture.”
teach: Say: “The last chapters of the Bible, Revelation 21-22, describe a new creation: ‘Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.’ The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down from God. ‘Behold, the dwelling of God is with men.’ Isaiah 65:17 and 2 Peter 3:13 also speak of ‘new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.’ The Church teaches that creation itself will be renewed: the material world is not discarded but transformed (Romans 8:19-23: creation groans, waiting for liberation). Heaven isn’t a disembodied existence, but the fulfillment of all things in Christ.”

Say: “The resurrection of the body. The Creed: ‘I believe in the resurrection of the body and life everlasting.’ At the last day, Christ will raise the dead; our bodies will be reunited with our souls, glorified (1 Corinthians 15:35-53). The resurrected body is the same body, yet transformed, ‘imperishable,’ ‘spiritual.’ Jesus’ risen body is the model: it could be touched, eat fish, yet pass through doors. The Church teaches that all will rise, the just and the unjust (John 5:28-29). This means that the body has dignity. It is why the Church honors the bodies of the dead and prefers burial. It rejects both pure materialism (death is the end) and the notion that the soul alone matters (Gnosticism, reincarnation).”

Say: “What will heaven be like? We don’t know in detail, but the images: a wedding feast (Revelation 19:9), a city of light, a garden, perfect friendship, rest and work, worship, learning. The Church teaches that we will recognize loved ones; we will be perfected in our individuality. Gregory’s insight: because God is infinite, our growth in him never ends. The joy increases forever. Hope for the new creation changes how we live now: we work for justice and care for creation because they anticipate the Kingdom (Vatican II, GS 39: the good fruits of human work will be found again, purified, in the new earth). We pray ‘Thy kingdom come.’ We live in hope: ‘Maranatha, Come, Lord Jesus.’ The Catechism ends with ‘Amen’: so be it.”
ask: What does Revelation 21 describe? (A new heaven, new earth and the holy city.)
What does the Church teach about the resurrection of the body? (We will rise with glorified bodies at the last day.)
What is epektasis? (Endless growth into God.)
practice: Draw a picture or write a description of the new creation using only images from Scripture.
Explain the resurrection of the body in two sentences for a friend.
List three things you do now that anticipate the Kingdom.
Write a short prayer of hope.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Lord Jesus.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Revelation 21:1-7 aloud.”

tryit: Describe the new creation using Scripture.
Explain the resurrection of the body.
Write what you hope for.
lessons.saintStory:
Gregory of Nyssa, born around 335, was the younger brother of Basil the Great and Macrina. He was trained as a teacher of rhetoric, and was married. Basil persuaded him to become bishop of Nyssa, a small town, in 372. He was a gentle man, not suited to church politics, and was falsely accused of embezzlement by supporters of Arian emperor Valens and driven out in 376, but returned in 378 after the emperor’s death.
At the Council of Constantinople in 381, he was recognized as a pillar of the faith, and he helped to shape the Nicene Creed. He wrote on the Trinity, the soul, the resurrection, and the spiritual life. In his Life of Moses, he described the spiritual life as an endless journey. Moses, he said, always went further into the darkness of God. This is called epektasis: “stretching forward.” Even in heaven, the soul never exhausts God, but grows forever in love and knowledge.
He died around 395. His brother Basil built the Church’s institutions; Gregory contemplated its depths.

units.title: Mission
units.eq: How do I live my faith now?

lessons.title: Lay mission
lessons.idea: Laypeople are the Church in the world. Through Baptism they share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly mission, and their special vocation is to sanctify the world from within: in family, work, culture and public life.
lessons.question: What is my mission?
lessons.activity: “Write a mission statement” (45 min). Students write a one-page personal mission statement for their lay vocation: values, relationships, work, parish, service. They name three concrete commitments and a person who will hold them accountable.
teach: The laity “seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to God’s will” (CCC 898; Lumen Gentium 31). Apostolicam Actuositatem (the Decree on the Lay Apostolate) elaborates this.
They share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office (CCC 901–913). They can also serve in parish ministries.
Examples: St Thomas More (politics), St Gianna Beretta Molla (medicine, motherhood), Blessed Frédéric Ozanam (charity), St Josemaría Escrivá (sanctifying work).
Avoid clericalizing the laity. Their mission belongs to them by Baptism.
talk: What is the mission of the laity?
quiz: Lay people share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly mission by…|Only joining parish committees|Taking over clerical duties|Staying out of society|Consecrating the world from within through work, family and civic life (CCC 898–900)|3|CCC 898–913.
Which is an accurate description of the laity’s role?|Active members with a mission of their own by Baptism|Servants of clergy only|Passive|Optional in the Church|0|CCC 897–913.

An example of lay holiness in public life is…|An angel|Jerome, only a hermit|Francis, who rejected all work|Thomas More, who served as a statesman and died for conscience|3|Examples of lay sanctity in public life.
lessons.saint: Blessed Ceferino Giménez Malla: a Roma horse-trader and layman who was shot rather than give up his rosary.
misc: “The laity’s role is to pray, pay and obey.”
lessons.mem: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:13–16 (salt and light). Ask: “Where are you called to be salt and light this year?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present their mission statement and one commitment.

script.open: Write on the board the sentence, ‘Mission is for missionaries.’ Invite students to stand at one side of the room if they agree and the other if they disagree. Ask one person from each side to explain.
teach: Say: “Jesus’ great commission was given to all the baptized. Vatican II’s Apostolicam Actuositatem (1965) is the decree on the lay apostolate: ‘The Christian vocation is, of its very nature, a vocation to the apostolate.’ The laity share in the Church’s mission by virtue of Baptism and Confirmation. Their field is the world: the temporal order. ‘By their very vocation, lay people seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to the plan of God.’ (LG 31) The call to holiness and the call to mission are the same call. John Paul II’s Christifideles Laici (1988) calls the laity to a new evangelization: ‘Go into my vineyard too.’”

Say: “Forms of lay mission. Witness of life: family, work, friendships; living the Gospel visibly. Evangelization: sharing the faith by word. Service: works of mercy, charity, volunteering. Social and political engagement: justice, advocacy, public life. Ministry within the Church: catechists, readers, music, youth leaders, parish councils, campus ministry. Professional apostolate: doctors, lawyers, teachers, artists. Movements: Catholic Action, St. Vincent de Paul Society, Knights of Columbus, Focolare, Communion and Liberation, Opus Dei, Neocatechumenal Way, Catholic Worker, FOCUS, NET, Life Teen, Young Catholic Professionals. Each person has charisms (1 Corinthians 12). Find yours.”

Say: “How to start. Pray: discern where God calls. Learn: know your faith. Join: a parish group, a campus ministry, a service organization. Serve: begin small and local. Invite: a friend to Mass, a retreat or an event. Be consistent: mission is a way of life. Obstacles: fear, shyness, busyness, discouragement. The Spirit gives courage. Pope Francis: ‘I am a mission on this earth; that is the reason why I am here in this world.’ (Evangelii Gaudium 273) Ceferino had no formal education or high status, yet he lived his faith by honesty, prayer and courage. He bore witness to Christ among both his own people and others. A plan for next year: choose one way to serve, one way to grow, and one way to invite.”
ask: What is the lay apostolate? (The laity’s share in the Church’s mission.)
What is the laity’s special field? (The world: family, work, culture, politics.)
Name three forms of lay mission. (Witness, service, ministry, social engagement.)
practice: Make a mission plan: one way to serve, one way to grow, one way to invite.
For each, write who, what, when.
Identify a group you can join: parish, campus, service organization.
Share your plan with a partner who will check in.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, send me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Take the first step in your mission plan this week.”

tryit: Describe a lay apostolate you could do.
Match it to a gift and a need.
Write a one-year plan.
lessons.saintStory:
Ceferino Giménez Malla, nicknamed El Pelé, was born in 1861 in Catalonia, Spain, to a Roma (Gypsy) family. He grew up traveling and became a successful horse trader. He was married in a Catholic ceremony to Teresa Giménez Castro, and they had no children, but adopted a niece. He could not read or write, but was known for honesty, generosity to the poor and love for the faith.
He went to Mass often, prayed the Rosary daily, and was a member of the Conference of St. Vincent de Paul. He helped settle disputes among his people and acted as a bridge between the Roma and others. He once helped a priest who was being attacked by a mob and was in turn arrested for defending him.
In July 1936, at the start of the Spanish Civil War, anti-Church violence swept Barbastro. Ceferino was arrested for protecting a priest and for carrying a rosary. He was offered release if he gave up his rosary. He refused. On August 9, 1936, he was shot, crying “Long live Christ the King!” He was seventy-five. In 1997, John Paul II beatified him, the first Roma person to be beatified.

lessons.title: Prayer for life
lessons.idea: A rule of life is a realistic plan for daily and weekly practices that keep a person close to God: Mass, Confession, daily prayer, Scripture, service, rest, and community. It brings structure so love can grow.
lessons.question: What is my rule?
lessons.activity: “Create a rule of life” (45 min). Students draft a rule with daily (Morning Offering, Scripture, Angelus or short prayer, Examen), weekly (Sunday Mass, a service act, a rest day), monthly (Confession, a retreat or spiritual reading), yearly (a retreat). They share it with a friend or mentor and set a review date.
teach: A rule of life gives order and consistency to the Christian life, as in religious orders and in lay associations (CCC 2030). It should be realistic, flexible and revisable.
Prayer is essential: “pray constantly” (1 Thessalonians 5:17; CCC 2742–2745). The sacraments, especially Eucharist and Penance, nourish. Scripture forms mind and heart.
Acts of service and rest keep the rule balanced. Spiritual direction helps keep it honest.
Teach perseverance: relapse and restart are normal. Grace comes before and after effort.
talk: What do you need in a rule?
quiz: A good rule of life is best described as…|A rigid set of rules to earn salvation|An optional hobby|A realistic, flexible plan of practices that supports love of God and neighbor|A secret code|2|CCC 2030, 2044.
Which element is essential in any Catholic rule of life?|Silence|Weekly Sunday Mass and regular sacramental life|Daily fasting|Travel|1|CCC 2042–2043.
What should you do when you fail to keep your rule?|Blame others|Give up|Hide it|Begin again without drama and adjust it|3|The goal is love, not perfection.
lessons.saint: Venerable Madeleine Delbrêl: an atheist teenager who became a social worker and a mystic in a Communist suburb of Paris.
misc: “Anything less than an hour of prayer a day doesn’t count.”
lessons.mem: “Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 18:1: “Jesus told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.” Ask: “What helps you keep a habit?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to present their rule and explain how it supports love of God and neighbor.

script.open: Ring a small bell or play a chime. Say, “In monasteries, a bell like this stops everything for prayer. What would it take to stop your day for prayer?” Take quick answers, then ring it again and pray a line together.
teach: Say: “Prayer is the lifeblood of mission. Without it, work becomes activism, and mission dry. Jesus himself went off to pray (Mark 1:35), spent nights in prayer before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12), and prayed at Gethsemane. The Church’s tradition of prayer includes the Liturgy: Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours; personal prayer; popular devotions. The Catechism says prayer is ‘the habit of being in the presence of the thrice-holy God and in communion with him.’ (CCC 2565) We pray ‘at all times’ (Ephesians 6:18). A person of prayer sees the world differently. The Church distinguishes the active and contemplative life, but both are needed. Mary and Martha: Jesus said, ‘Mary has chosen the good portion’ (Luke 10:42), not to dismiss service but to say it must flow from listening.”

Say: “Madeleine Delbrêl lived prayer in the city. She wrote, ‘We, the ordinary people of the streets.’ She said that a person can pray anywhere by offering each task, by short prayers, and by seeing Christ in others. She wrote a ‘Rule of life’ including: a morning offering; the Gospel read daily; silence; the Mass; the Our Father said slowly. A practical daily rhythm: Morning: offering and a short Scripture. Midday: Angelus or pause. Evening: examination of conscience and gratitude. Night: Compline or the Our Father. Weekly: Sunday Mass; Confession monthly; time before the Blessed Sacrament. Seasonal: retreats, days of recollection, Lent and Advent practices. Pray with others: a prayer group, Bible study, family prayer.”

Say: “Prayer for life: asking God’s help for our needs and for others. The Church’s teaching on intercession: Jesus invites us to ask (Matthew 7:7-11; John 16:23-24). God knows our needs, but wants us to ask; prayer changes us, aligns our will, and God may use our prayer to accomplish good. Unanswered prayer: sometimes God says no or wait; Paul’s thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). Jesus in Gethsemane: ‘Not my will, but yours.’ A prayer for life includes: praying for the sick, the dying, the unborn, for vocations, for peace, and for the Church. The Rosary is a prayer for life. The Church also prays with the great prayers: the Our Father (the model), the Hail Mary, the Creed, and the Psalms. Let prayer be a lifeline of your mission.”
ask: What does the Catechism say prayer is? (Being in God’s presence and communion with him.)
What does ‘the street is our cloister’ mean? (We can find God in daily work and city life.)
Why pray for others? (Jesus invites us, and God uses our prayer.)
practice: Design your own rule of prayer: a morning, midday, evening and weekly pattern.
Choose one practice that you will commit to for 30 days.
Identify an obstacle and a plan to handle it.
Share with an accountability partner.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly, line by line. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Try your prayer rule for a month.”

tryit: Design a daily rhythm of prayer.
Include a time in the city.
Choose one practice to start.
lessons.saintStory:
Madeleine Delbrêl was born in 1904 in France. As a teenager, she was a brilliant, lively atheist. She wrote at seventeen, “God is dead… long live death.” But she was a sincere seeker. When her friend and fiancé Jean entered the Dominicans, she was shaken, and began, at twenty, to study seriously the faith of her friends. One night, in 1924, she knelt to pray. She wrote that she discovered God exists, and that she wanted to live for him: “God is alive.”
She trained as a social worker and in 1933 moved with two friends to Ivry-sur-Seine, a working-class suburb of Paris run by the Communist Party. They formed a small community of lay women, la Charité de Jésus, living the Gospel in the streets. She worked as a municipal social worker and spent time with workers, Communists and the poor. She prayed hours each day, joining contemplation and action.
She wrote about finding God in daily life: “The street is our cloister.” She died in 1964. In 2018 she was declared Venerable.

lessons.title: Sending forth
lessons.idea: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” As graduates and young adults, students are sent. The Church’s mission is carried out by missionary disciples who witness with their lives and words, wherever they go.
lessons.question: How will I go?
lessons.activity: “Commissioning” (45 min). Hold a simple commissioning rite: reading, a moment where each student names their commitment aloud, a blessing, the Sending Forth, a prayer. Provide a symbolic gift (a cross, a small Bible, a prayer card). Close with a hymn.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–851; Ad Gentes 2). Evangelization includes witness of life, proclamation, dialogue, works of charity (CCC 2044).
Pope Francis (Evangelii Gaudium) speaks of “missionary disciples.” Every Christian is both disciple and missionary.
Go with humility, joy, courage and openness. The Spirit goes before.
Remain connected to the Church community: parish, campus ministry, young adult groups.

The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20) includes…|Go, make disciples, baptize, teach, and the promise “I am with you always”|A command to avoid people|Only teaching|Only baptizing|0|Matthew 28:19–20.
Which approach to sharing faith fits Catholic teaching?|Imposing|Witness, gentleness, truth and respect for freedom (1 Peter 3:15; CCC 160)|Pressure and argument|Silence|1|CCC 160, 2104–2109.
lessons.life: Pray for the grace to be sent.
lessons.saint: Saint Lorenzo Ruiz: a married Filipino layman and father of three who died in Nagasaki rather than renounce his faith.
misc: “Mission is only for those who go overseas.”
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit… and behold, I am with you always.” (Matthew 28:19–20)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 28:19–20. Ask: “What are the verbs? What is the promise?” Go, make disciples, baptize, teach; and “I am with you always.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state their commitments to mission after graduation.

script.open: Ask, “What is the last thing you want to hear at the end of Mass? ‘Go in peace’? Why do you think the Mass ends with a command?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Mass ends with a dismissal: ‘Go forth, the Mass is ended,’ or ‘Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord.’ In Latin, ‘Ite, missa est’; the word ‘Mass’ comes from missa, ‘sent.’ The liturgy culminates in mission. We are sent to bring Christ to the world. The Church’s own nature is missionary (Ad Gentes 2): ‘The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature.’ Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium: ‘In virtue of their baptism, all the members of the People of God have become missionary disciples.’ The same Christ who calls us, sends us.”

Say: “Sending in Scripture. Isaiah: ‘Whom shall I send?… Here am I! Send me.’ Jeremiah, Jonah, Mary, the apostles. The Twelve and then seventy-two sent out in pairs (Luke 10:1-12) with little baggage.
