After the Resurrection: ‘As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.’ (John 20:21) The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19-20) ends with the promise: ‘I am with you always.’ Confirmation: we receive the Spirit to witness. The Church has a long history of sending: the Apostles; Patrick, Boniface, Cyril and Methodius; Francis Xavier; the Maryknoll missionaries. Catholic missions today: Catholic Relief Services, Missionary Societies, lay missionaries, Mission Co-op Sundays, World Mission Sunday. Each parish is a base for mission.”

Say: “A final reflection. Your faith journey doesn’t end with graduation from Catholic school or religious education. You are being sent into college, work, military, family, friendships. Questions to carry: Will I go to Mass on Sunday? Will I find a community? Will I keep praying? Will I continue to learn? Will I serve? Will I invite? Will I be honest and loving? Will I come back to Confession when I fall? Practical: find a campus ministry or young adult group, a spiritual mentor, a Bible study, a service project. Mission isn’t about perfection but fidelity. Lorenzo Ruiz did not begin as a hero; he was a husband and father who found himself tested. At the dismissal, we’re told: ‘Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.’”
ask: What does ‘Mass’ come from? (Missa, ‘sent.’)
What did Jesus say at the end of Matthew’s Gospel? (I am with you always.)
What can you do after graduation to stay in the faith? (Find community, pray, serve, go to Mass and Confession.)
practice: Write your own sending prayer: ‘Lord, I am sent to…’
Write the three places you will be sent in the next year, and one commitment for each.
Choose a symbol or object to remind you (a cross, a medal, a verse).
Share one commitment aloud.
script.close: Pray together the dismissal: “Go in peace, glorifying the Lord by your life.” Answer: “Thanks be to God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find a Catholic community at your next school or workplace.”

tryit: Write your own sending prayer.
Name where you will be sent.
Pick a symbol of your mission.
lessons.saintStory:
Lorenzo Ruiz was born around 1600 in Manila, to a Chinese father and Tagalog mother, both Catholics. He was educated by the Dominicans in Binondo, served as an altar boy and sacristan, and became a skilled calligrapher, copying documents for the Dominicans. He married and had two sons and a daughter. He was devout and joined the Confraternity of the Rosary.
In 1636, he was falsely accused of a crime, perhaps of a murder, and, in danger, he took refuge on a ship with three Dominican priests who were sailing to Japan, where Christianity was banned. They landed at Okinawa, where they were arrested and sent to Nagasaki.
The authorities tortured them, with water forced into the mouth and bamboo under the fingernails, to make them renounce the faith. Lorenzo wavered for a moment, then declared, “I am a Catholic, and I will die for God; if I had a thousand lives, all would be offered to Him.” He was hung upside down in a pit with a stone on his chest, and died on September 29, 1637. He was canonized in 1987, the first Filipino saint.

lessons.title: Review of the Creed
lessons.idea: The Creed is the summary of the faith. Reviewing it article by article helps students see how doctrine fits together and how it shapes life. Each student writes a commentary on the Creed in their own words.
lessons.question: What do I believe?
lessons.activity: “Write my own creed commentary” (50 min). Students choose two articles (e.g., “maker of heaven and earth”; “he descended to the dead”; “communion of saints”) and write a half-page each: what it says, Scripture, a Catechism reference, what difference it makes to my life. Recite the Creed together.
teach: The Creed organizes the faith: Father, Son, Holy Spirit and the Church (CCC 185–197). It is both a summary of faith and a personal profession.
The Creed has twelve articles in the Apostles’ Creed, traditionally attributed to the apostles (CCC 194). The Nicene Creed adds precision on Christ’s divinity and the Spirit.
Doctrine is connected to prayer and morals; lex orandi, lex credendi, lex vivendi.
Encourage students to pray the Creed regularly, e.g., at Mass, with attention.
quiz: The Apostles’ Creed is organized around…|Seven sacraments|Ten Commandments|The three Persons of the Trinity|Four marks|2|CCC 190.
The phrase “consubstantial with the Father” in the Nicene Creed teaches that…|The Son shares the same divine nature as the Father|Mary is divine|The Spirit is a force|The Son is a creature|0|CCC 242.

Why do we say “I believe” at Baptism but “We believe” at Mass?|It is accidental|The priests decide|Languages differ|Faith is personal and also shared with the whole Church (CCC 166–167)|3|CCC 166–167.
lessons.saint: The Twelve Apostles: an old tradition says each contributed one article of the Creed.
misc: “The Creed is an old formula with no relevance.”
“I can pick which articles to believe.”
lessons.mem: “If you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” (Romans 10:9)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 10:9. Ask: “What do you confess with your lips? What do you believe in your heart?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to share one article of the Creed and what it means for their life.

script.open: Ask the class to stand and say the Apostles’ Creed from memory, as far as they can. Notice the places where voices drop out, and write those lines on the board as the places to focus on.
teach: Say: “Review. The Creed has three parts, as in Baptism: I believe in God the Father, in Jesus Christ the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. First, the Father: God is one, almighty, Creator. The universe is a gift; humans are made in his image; evil entered through sin, not God’s will. Second, Jesus Christ: eternal Son, born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, truly God and truly man; suffered and died under Pontius Pilate to save us from sin; descended to the dead; rose on the third day; ascended to the Father; will come to judge. Third, the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who inspired the prophets, dwells in the Church; the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body; life everlasting.”

Say: “Sorting the Creed into central points. The Trinity. The Incarnation. The Paschal Mystery (Passion, death, Resurrection). The Church. The last things. Each connects to the others. Reviewing the story: Creation, fall, covenant, Christ, Church, new creation. The Creed is the story of salvation in short. Also, review how we know: Scripture, Tradition and Magisterium; faith and reason; reading the Bible in context; the councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon) that shaped the Creed. Also: Mary (Immaculate Conception, Mother of God, Assumption). The Creed is not just a list but a relationship: ‘I believe in’ means trust in a Person, not just assent to propositions.”

Say: “The Creed and life. Every article has consequences. God the Father: trust, gratitude, stewardship. Jesus the Son: discipleship, imitation, hope. The Holy Spirit: prayer, gifts, mission. The Church: belonging, obedience, service. Communion of saints: friendship with the saints and prayer for the dead. Forgiveness: Confession. Resurrection: hope, dignity of the body. Life everlasting: meaning in suffering and death. As you prepare your capstone statement of faith, think about how each part of the Creed shapes how you live. The Creed was a living confession for martyrs. It isn’t finished once you say it; it’s a life to be lived. ‘I believe; help my unbelief.’”
ask: What are the three parts of the Creed? (Father, Son, Holy Spirit.)
Which council wrote the Nicene Creed? (Nicaea and Constantinople.)
What does ‘I believe in’ mean? (Trust in a Person, not only agreement with statements.)
practice: Write each article of the Apostles’ Creed on a card.
On the back, write one Scripture text and one sentence of explanation.
Rank the articles by how clear they are to you, and mark the two you want to study more.
Share your list with a partner and trade explanations.
script.close: Pray the Apostles’ Creed together, slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Write your own one-sentence version of each part of the Creed.”

tryit: Explain each article of the Creed in one sentence.
Link each to a Scripture text.
Pick the one that matters most to you.
lessons.saintStory:
Around the year 400, a priest named Rufinus of Aquileia wrote a commentary on the Apostles’ Creed. He passed on an old tradition: after Pentecost, the apostles were about to scatter in mission. Before leaving Jerusalem, they met to agree on what they would all teach, a “rule of faith,” so that they would not preach different things. Led by the Holy Spirit, each contributed an article.
Later versions of the story assign the articles to the apostles by name. Peter: “I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” Andrew: “and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” James: “who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” John: “suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried.” And so on to Matthias: “life everlasting.”
Historians doubt that the apostles composed the Creed in this way. The Creed grew out of baptismal professions in Rome over the first centuries. But the legend expresses a truth: the Creed faithfully sums up what the apostles taught. “This is the faith of the Church,” the Catechism says, “and it is the faith of all.”

lessons.title: Review of sacraments and morals
lessons.idea: This lesson integrates the sacraments and the moral life: grace received in the sacraments strengthens the life of love lived in the commandments and Beatitudes. Students present what they have learned and its coherence.
lessons.question: What changed?
lessons.activity: “Presentation” (50 min). In groups, students prepare a short presentation connecting a sacrament to a moral theme (Eucharist and justice; Penance and truth; Matrimony and chastity; Orders and service). They use Scripture, Catechism sections and a real-life example. Peers give feedback.
teach: The sacraments are the principal means of grace; the moral life is the response (CCC 1210–1211, 1716, 2052). Grace heals and elevates, the commandments and Beatitudes direct.
The Catechism has four pillars: Creed, sacraments, commandments, prayer. They interlock: what we believe, celebrate, live and pray.
Sacramental grace is not a license but a power: the Eucharist makes us one body and sends us.
Encourage students to find the thread through the whole course.
quiz: Grace and the moral life relate as…|Grace makes commandments unnecessary|Grace heals and strengthens us to live the commandments and Beatitudes|Only one matters|Law replaces grace|1|CCC 1996–2005.
The Catechism’s four parts correspond to…|Faith professed, celebrated, lived and prayed|Four councils|Genesis to Revelation|Four gospels|0|CCC 13–18.
Which sacrament strengthens us most directly for the moral life of charity?|None|The Eucharist, which makes us one body and sends us out|Only Baptism|Only Confirmation|1|CCC 1391–1397.
lessons.saint: John Baptist de La Salle: a priest who gave away his fortune to start schools and taught teachers how to teach the faith.
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God… and your neighbor as yourself.” (Matthew 22:37–39)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 22:37–40. Ask: “How do the sacraments help us live these two commands?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how a sacrament strengthens a moral virtue with a concrete example.

script.open: Divide the board in half and write ‘sacraments’ on one side and ‘morals’ on the other. Give teams two minutes to write as many key terms as they can on each side. Count, compare and note the gaps.
teach: Say: “Review of the sacraments. Initiation: Baptism (new birth, forgiveness, incorporation), Confirmation (the Spirit’s seal for witness), Eucharist (source and summit; sacrifice, real presence, communion). Healing: Reconciliation (contrition, confession, satisfaction, absolution), Anointing (strength in illness). Service: Holy Orders (bishop, priest, deacon; acting in persona Christi), Matrimony (covenant; spouses are ministers; unity, indissolubility, openness to life). Each has matter, form, minister and effect. Which can be received only once: Baptism, Confirmation, Orders (they imprint a character). How they work: ex opere operato, with the disposition of the recipient. Who is the minister of each? Know the answers.”

Say: “Review of morals. The foundation: dignity of the person, made in God’s image; the Beatitudes as our end; freedom and responsibility; the three sources of morality (object, intention, circumstances); conscience formed by the Church’s teaching; law (eternal, natural, Old, New); sin (mortal and venial; the capital sins); grace and the virtues (theological and cardinal). The Ten Commandments: love of God (no other gods; the name; the Lord’s Day) and neighbor (family; life; chastity; justice; truth; purity of heart; detachment). Catholic social teaching: dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, the option for the poor, stewardship of creation. Apply to cases: life, marriage and sexuality, justice, war and peace.”

Say: “Study methods for review. Use the Catechism of the Catholic Church’s Compendium. Make flashcards. Work in pairs and quiz each other. Make a one-page ‘map’ connecting sacraments, virtues and commandments. Explain a topic to a younger student; teaching is the best test. Link each doctrine to Scripture and to a saint. Distinguish ‘what the Church teaches’ from opinion. Identify gaps and plan to fill them. De La Salle’s approach: clear, patient, adapted to the student. A Catholic in the world needs to be able to explain. Pope Francis: ‘Be prepared… be brave.’ Your capstone is a chance to show this.”
ask: Which three sacraments leave a character? (Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders.)
What are the three sources of morality? (Object, intention, circumstances.)
What are the principles of Catholic social teaching? (Dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, option for the poor, stewardship.)
practice: Draw a one-page map with the seven sacraments at the center, connected to virtues, commandments and Scripture.
Mark with a star the three items you know best and a question mark on the three you know least.
Quiz a partner with five questions each.
Plan how to fill your gaps before the capstone.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make me a clear and faithful witness.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Teach one topic to a family member.”

tryit: Make a one-page map of the sacraments and morals.
Connect each sacrament to a virtue and a commandment.
Identify your gaps.
lessons.saintStory:
John Baptist de La Salle was born in 1651 in Reims, France, the oldest of ten children of a wealthy family. He studied for the priesthood and became a canon of the cathedral at twenty-seven. In 1679, he met a man named Adrien Nyel, who was starting free schools for poor boys. At first, John only helped, but he saw that the teachers were poorly trained, and he began to take them into his home and train them.
Gradually he gave himself fully. He resigned his canonry, and in 1684 distributed his wealth to the poor during a famine. He founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools, a community of lay teachers. He developed new methods: teaching in French instead of Latin, grouping students by ability, teaching in classes rather than one by one, and including religion. He wrote the Conduct of Schools.
He died in 1719. In 1900 he was canonized, and in 1950 named patron of teachers. His life shows that clear teaching is a work of love.

lessons.title: Capstone presentation
lessons.idea: The capstone is a final project in which students share what they have learned, how it has changed them and how they plan to live it, including a prayer. It is a chance to take ownership of faith as adults.
lessons.question: What is next?
lessons.activity: “Capstone project” (a week of preparation; 60 min sessions). Each student creates a project: a written reflection, a video, a service initiative, an artwork, or a teaching session. It includes: three key insights, one challenge or question, a plan for next steps and a prayer. Present to the class or parish, with a closing blessing.
teach: A capstone integrates learning, as in Catechism’s structure (CCC 2030). It invites personal appropriation: “faith seeking understanding.”
Include a plan: sacraments, service, study, community, mentor. A plan needs accountability.
The prayer is part of the work: thanksgiving, petition, offering.
Celebrate: an agape meal or a Mass of thanksgiving would be fitting.
quiz: A well-formed personal capstone plan includes…|Only ideas|Insights, a concrete plan, support and a prayer|A grade only|Nothing|1|Integrated learning leads to action.
Which best describes the aim of Christian formation?|Becoming disciples who know, celebrate, live and pray the faith|Memorizing facts only|Winning arguments|Earning credit|0|CCC 4–6.
After graduation, a student should stay connected to…|A single teacher|A parish, community and mentors|No one|Only social media|1|The faith is lived in the Church.
lessons.saint: Paul at Miletus: “I have finished the race.”
misc: “The end of the course is the end of formation.”
lessons.mem: “Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)
lessons.hook: Read Philippians 3:12–14. Ask: “What does Paul mean by pressing on toward the goal?” Ask students what they hope to carry forward.
lessons.assess: Evaluate capstones using a rubric: accuracy, depth, personal engagement, concrete plan and prayer.

script.open: Say, “You’re about to give your statement of faith. Take a moment to think: if a friend asked, ‘What do you believe, and why does it matter to you?’, what would you want to be able to say in three minutes?” Let students write silently for two minutes.
teach: Say: “A statement of faith is a personal, honest account of what you believe, why and how it shapes your life. It is not a recitation of the Creed, but your own voice in harmony with the Church’s faith. Ancient examples: the confession of Peter (Matthew 16:16); the martyrs’ responses at trial; Augustine’s Confessions; Thérèse’s Story of a Soul; Newman’s Apologia; Paul’s speech at Miletus. Elements: what I believe (a section drawn from the Creed), why I believe (reasons, experiences, witnesses), how I live it (practices, commitments), and what I hope for (the future).”

Say: “Plan your presentation. One: Opening: a story or question that draws attention. Two: Core beliefs: pick three to five central truths, such as that God is Father, Jesus is Lord, the Church is his Body, the sacraments give grace, I am called to love. Three: Evidence and reasons: Scripture, reason, the lives of saints, personal experience. Four: Challenge: name a doubt or difficulty you have faced, and how you worked through it; being honest makes it credible. Five: Commitment: what you will do, specifically, in the next year. Six: Closing: a prayer or Scripture. Keep it to about three to five minutes. Practice aloud. Be yourself. Use notes if you need them.”

Say: “Expectations. Be accurate: check the Catechism. Be clear: explain terms. Be personal: speak from your heart. Be respectful: of those who disagree. Be brief. Listeners: listen attentively, respond with encouragement, ask a question, and affirm. Close with a prayer for one another. Remember Paul’s words: ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.’ You haven’t finished the race, but you can say, ‘I press on toward the goal.’ (Philippians 3:14) The faith is a gift to be handed on. Thank those who taught you. Celebrate. This is not the end, but a sending forth.”
ask: What are the parts of a statement of faith? (What I believe, why, how I live it, what I hope for.)
How long should the presentation be? (About three to five minutes.)
What should listeners do? (Listen, encourage, ask a question.)
practice: Write an outline of your statement: opening, core beliefs, reasons, a difficulty, a commitment, closing.
Rehearse it aloud to a partner, timing it.
Revise based on feedback.
Present to the class (or in small groups) and respond to questions.
script.close: Pray together a prayer of blessing for the class, ending with the Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank someone who passed the faith to you, in writing.”

tryit: Outline your statement of faith.
Add a story and a Scripture.
Rehearse a three-minute version.
lessons.saintStory:
Near the end of his third missionary journey, Paul wanted to hurry to Jerusalem. He stopped at Miletus, a port near Ephesus, and sent for the elders of the Ephesian church to meet him. His farewell to them in Acts 20 is the only speech of Paul to Christians in the Acts.
He reminded them of how he had lived among them for three years, serving the Lord with humility and tears, teaching in public and from house to house. He told them he was going to Jerusalem, “constrained by the Spirit,” not knowing what would happen, except that “in every city the Holy Spirit testifies to me that imprisonment and afflictions await me.” He added, “But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may accomplish my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.”
He warned them to guard the flock, and entrusted them to God. They wept, embraced him and kissed him, grieving most that they would not see him again. Years later, from prison in Rome, he wrote: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” (2 Timothy 4:7)

units.title: Hard questions: justice, science and salvation
units.eq: How do I hold to the faith when the issues are difficult?

lessons.title: The death penalty, war and peace
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that the death penalty is “inadmissible” today because of the dignity of the person, and that war may only be a last resort and must meet strict conditions.
lessons.question: Can killing ever be justified?
lessons.activity: Hold a structured debate using the just war criteria.
teach: In 2018 Pope Francis revised CCC 2267: the death penalty is “inadmissible” because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. Earlier editions allowed it in very rare cases if it was the only way to protect lives. The Church works for abolition.

Legitimate defense may require force (CCC 2263–2265) and bear grave responsibility. A war may only be just if: lasting, grave damage by an aggressor; all other means impractical; serious prospects of success; the use of arms does not produce greater evils (CCC 2309).
Conscientious objection is respected and those who serve are to see themselves as servants of peace (CCC 2310–2311).
Faithful Catholics argue about how to apply these principles. Study the criteria before taking a side.
talk: What does it mean that every life has dignity, even a murderer’s?
Is a “just war” possible in the age of nuclear weapons?
How should the justice owed to victims be balanced with mercy?
quiz: What did the 2018 revision of CCC 2267 say?|The Church takes no position|The death penalty is required|The death penalty is inadmissible|It is allowed whenever the state chooses|2|The revision.
Which is NOT one of the conditions for a just war?|A declaration by a popular vote|Lasting, grave damage by an aggressor|All other means impractical|Serious prospects of success|0|CCC 2309.
The Church’s view of conscientious objectors is that…|They deserve respect and a way to serve|They are heretics|They are always wrong|They must be punished|0|CCC 2311.
lessons.life: Read a short Church document on peace or the death penalty and share one question.
lessons.saint: Jacques Fesch: a murderer who converted in prison and went to the guillotine with faith.
misc: “The Church has always taught the death penalty is wrong.”
“Any war is justified if the government declares it.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the peacemakers.” (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When is it right to use force? When is it never right?” List answers before the criteria.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state why the Church calls the death penalty inadmissible and apply the just war criteria to a case.

script.open: Say carefully, “This lesson involves violence and killing. We keep in mind victims and their families.” Ask, “What is punishment for? Revenge, protection, deterrence, or rehabilitation?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Catechism on the death penalty. Traditionally, the Church recognized that public authority could, in cases of extreme gravity, impose the death penalty if it was the only practical way to defend human life against an unjust aggressor. But in 2018 Pope Francis revised paragraph 2267: ‘Recourse to the death penalty on the part of legitimate authority, following a fair trial, was long considered an appropriate response to the gravity of certain crimes… Today, however, there is an increasing awareness that the dignity of the person is not lost even after the commission of very serious crimes… Consequently, the Church teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that ‘the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,’ and she works with determination for its abolition worldwide.’ This is a development of doctrine, building on John Paul II’s Evangelium Vitae 56, which said that cases where execution is absolutely necessary ‘are very rare, if not practically non-existent.’”

Say: “Reasons given: modern prisons can protect society, making execution unnecessary; the risk of executing the innocent; unequal application by race and class; the dignity of every person, even the guilty; the chance for repentance; and that executions perpetuate violence. Objections: the demands of justice for the victims; deterrence; and that the Church historically accepted it. The Church replies that justice can be served by life imprisonment; the penalty should aim at the good of the offender and the community; mercy doesn’t cancel justice; and the Church has always sought the repentance of the guilty. Victims: the Church stands with victims and families, and recognizes their pain and need for justice. Many families find that execution doesn’t heal. Restorative justice approaches can help.”

Say: “War and peace (see Grade 12 unit 3). Just war criteria and modern war. The Catechism affirms legitimate defense. The Church condemns the targeting of civilians and weapons of mass destruction. Conscientious objection is honored. Issues: drones, cyber war, torture (never allowed), humanitarian intervention, refugees. Peacemaking: dialogue, justice and forgiveness. ‘The fruit of justice will be peace.’ (Isaiah 32:17) Jacques Fesch’s story raises a question: what do we owe those who have done terrible things? The Church answers: justice and mercy, protection of society, and hope for conversion. We also ask: do we see the dignity in every person? That includes victims first. And finally, there’s the question of how we respond to wrongs we ourselves suffer: forgiveness (Matthew 18:21-22; Luke 23:34). Forgiveness is not forgetting or excusing; it is choosing not to hate.”
ask: What does the Catechism now say of the death penalty? (It is inadmissible because it attacks the dignity of the person.)
What did John Paul II say about necessity? (Cases are rare, if not practically non-existent.)
What do we owe victims? (Justice, support and compassion.)
practice: Make a two-column chart: arguments for the death penalty and arguments against.
Add the Church’s response to each.
Write a paragraph defending the Church’s position respectfully to a friend who disagrees.
Write a prayer for victims and for the conversion of offenders.
script.close: Pray for victims and their families and for prisoners. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone in prison and for the families they harmed.”

tryit: Lay out the Church’s teaching on the death penalty.
State the strongest arguments on each side.
Write what mercy and justice each require.
lessons.saintStory:
Jacques Fesch was born in Paris in 1930, the son of a wealthy Belgian banker. He grew up in a household without warmth, left school early, and drifted. He married and had a daughter, but he abandoned his family because he wanted to sail to the South Pacific to find freedom. To pay for the boat, he planned a robbery of a currency exchange office in Paris on February 25, 1954. In the attempt, he shot and killed a police officer, Jean Vergnes, a husband and father. He was arrested, tried and sentenced to death.
In prison, he was an atheist, but his lawyer’s encouragement moved him. In 1954 he described a night of overwhelming experience in which he felt himself cry out for help and be seized by a hand. He began to read the Bible and to pray. He wrote many letters, later published as Light Over the Scaffold, speaking of peace and sorrow.
He was guillotined on October 1, 1957, at age twenty-seven. On the morning of his death he wrote in his notebook, “In five hours I will see Jesus!” Cardinal Lustiger of Paris opened his cause for canonization. His case shows both the gravity of his crime and the possibility of conversion. We pray also for the family of the officer he killed.

lessons.title: IVF, cloning and bioethics
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that children are a gift, not a product, and that science must serve the dignity of the person. It supports ethical treatments for infertility and rejects those that replace the marital act or destroy embryos.
lessons.question: Why does the Church say no to some fertility treatments?
lessons.activity: Compare ethical and unethical approaches in a table.
teach: The Church sympathizes deeply with couples who struggle with infertility (CCC 2374). It teaches that a child is a gift, not something owed or manufactured (CCC 2378).

In vitro fertilization separates procreation from the marital act and usually involves the creation and loss of embryos, so the Church holds that it is not morally acceptable (CCC 2377; Donum Vitae, 1987). Cloning and the destruction of embryos for research are rejected (CCC 2275).
Ethical options exist: restorative reproductive medicine, NFP-based fertility care, surgery and treatments that help the marital act, and also adoption and fostering and service (CCC 2379).
Adult stem cells and many other research paths are morally acceptable and effective.
talk: Why is it harder for a society to say “no” to technology that is wanted by many?
How can the Church speak with compassion to couples who have struggled with infertility?
What questions should we ask whenever science offers a new power?
quiz: A child conceived through IVF is…|A human person with full dignity|Less than human|Not loved by the Church|Not baptizable|0|The Church welcomes every child.
Which research is considered ethical?|None|Destroying embryos for stem cells|Cloning human embryos|Adult stem cell research|3|CCC 2275.
The Catechism’s advice to childless couples includes…|Pretending there is no pain|Adoption and service to others|Using any technology|Giving up on family|1|CCC 2379.
lessons.life: Pray for couples who are struggling to conceive or to adopt, and consider how you can support them.
lessons.saint: Joachim and Anne: according to tradition, an older couple without children who prayed and were heard.
misc: “The Church is against all fertility treatments and all stem cell research.”
“A child conceived through IVF is not a person.”
lessons.mem: “Children are a heritage from the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward.” (Psalm 127:3)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that infertility is a deep suffering for many couples. Begin with compassion.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why the Church distinguishes treatment from replacement of the marital act and name ethical options.

script.open: Say gently, “Many couples long for children and cannot have them. Our teaching must be firm and compassionate. Some here may have family who struggled.” Ask, “What do you think a couple longing for a child should be able to do? Are there limits?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church honors the desire for children as a good, and calls infertility a cross. Donum Vitae (1987) and Dignitas Personae (2008) explain the principles. First: a child is a gift, not a right or a product. Second: the child should be conceived in the marital act, as an expression of the spouses’ love, not made in a lab. The unitive and procreative meanings are united. So IVF (in vitro fertilization), where eggs are fertilized outside the body, is morally wrong in the Church’s teaching: it separates procreation from the conjugal act, often involves the creation of more embryos than are implanted, some of which are frozen or destroyed, and treats the child as a product. Surrogacy raises similar problems, and exploits women. Artificial insemination by a donor violates the marriage covenant. Cloning for reproduction or research is gravely wrong.”

Say: “What the Church supports: treatment that helps the marital act achieve its end, e.g., medical treatment of the causes of infertility such as hormone therapy, surgery for blocked tubes, treating endometriosis. NaProTechnology and Natural Family Planning methods to track fertility. Adoption and foster care: generous ways of parenthood. Spiritual fruitfulness: service, teaching, mentoring, godparenting. The Church recognizes that these teachings are painful for couples. A child conceived by IVF is a person with the same dignity: the child is not to blame. Pastoral care should be tender. Also, regarding embryos already frozen: a moral dilemma; the Church urges that they be respected, and the idea of ‘adoption’ of embryos remains debated.”

Say: “Related bioethics issues. Prenatal testing: acceptable for care, wrong if used to eliminate. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis: involves discarding embryos. Contraception and sterilization (see Grade 10). Gene editing: therapy is acceptable; enhancement and germline editing raise grave concerns. Stem cells (see above). Research on human subjects: informed consent, no harm. Organ donation: a gift. AI and genetics. How to discuss: with charity and clarity. The principle: ‘Is this respectful of the dignity of the person at every stage? Does it treat the person as a gift or a product?’ Dignitas Personae: ‘The Church… offers comfort and encouragement to couples who struggle with infertility.’ Joachim and Anne: faithful waiting; God’s gift in his time.”
ask: Why does the Church oppose IVF? (It separates procreation from the marital act and often destroys embryos.)
What does the Church support for infertile couples? (Treating causes, NaPro methods, adoption, spiritual fruitfulness.)
Does a child conceived by IVF have full dignity? (Yes.)
practice: Make a chart: Methods the Church accepts / Methods she doesn’t / Why.
Write a compassionate response to a friend whose cousin is using IVF.
List ways to support couples who struggle with infertility.
Compose a prayer for such couples.
script.close: Pray for couples longing for children and for children awaiting adoption. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Reach out kindly to someone who is struggling.”

tryit: Explain why the Church objects to IVF and cloning.
Explain what it supports for infertile couples.
Write a compassionate reply.
lessons.saintStory:
The Bible doesn’t name Mary’s parents. Their names, Joachim and Anne, come from an early Christian text, the Protoevangelium of James, from the second century. It is not Scripture, but the Church has honored these two as saints since ancient times, on July 26.
According to the story, Joachim was a wealthy and devout man whose offering at the Temple was rejected because he had no children. Humiliated, he went into the desert to fast and pray for forty days. Anne wept in her garden, lamenting that she was childless, comparing herself to the birds that have nests. An angel appeared to each, promising a child.
They conceived and named her Mary. When she was three, they brought her to the Temple, as they had vowed. This tradition echoes Hannah, mother of Samuel, and Sarah and Elizabeth, whose children were gifts after long waiting. For couples who struggle with infertility, Joachim and Anne are a patron.

lessons.title: Is there salvation outside the Church?
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that salvation comes through Christ and his Church, yet that God can lead those who do not know the Gospel through no fault of their own to salvation. It does not say who is saved or lost.
lessons.question: Does the Church say non-Catholics go to hell?
lessons.activity: Read Lumen Gentium 16 and write what it says in your own words.
teach: “Outside the Church there is no salvation” means that all salvation comes from Christ through his Church (CCC 846). It does not mean everyone outside the visible Church is lost.

Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ or his Church but seek God and try to do his will can be saved (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). The Church does not say how, but trusts in God’s mercy (CCC 1260).
This is why mission is not optional: the Church has the fullness of the means of salvation, and love compels us to share the Gospel (CCC 848).
The Church recognizes truth and holiness in other religions (CCC 843; Nostra Aetate) and respects each person’s conscience.
talk: If God can save people outside the Church, why does the Church send missionaries?
How is the Catholic view different from “all religions are the same”?
How should we speak about our friends who belong to other religions or none?
quiz: According to CCC 847, who can be saved?|Only the Church’s leaders|Only baptized Catholics|Those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ but seek God|No one outside the Church|2|CCC 847.
The Church’s teaching on mission is that…|The Gospel must be shared out of love|It is only for priests|It is forbidden|It is optional|0|CCC 848.
What does the Church say about other religions?|They may contain truth and holiness|They are identical to Christianity|They are worthless|They should be abolished|0|CCC 843.
lessons.life: Have a respectful conversation with someone of a different faith, asking what matters most to them.
lessons.saint: The Magi: foreigners who followed a star to Bethlehem.
misc: “The Church teaches that all non-Catholics are going to hell.”
“All religions are equally true, so it doesn’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you think Catholics believe happens to people of other faiths?” Collect answers before reading the Catechism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what the Church teaches about salvation outside the visible Church.

script.open: Ask, “What happens to a person who lived a good life but never heard of Jesus? What do you think the Church teaches? What do you hope?” Take honest answers.
teach: Say: “The Church holds two truths together. One: Christ is the only Savior; ‘there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved’ (Acts 4:12), and the Church is necessary for salvation (CCC 846). Two: God ‘desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth’ (1 Timothy 2:4). How do these fit? Lumen Gentium 14-16 and the Catechism 836-848: Those fully incorporated into the Church have the means of salvation in fullness. Baptized non-Catholics are in imperfect communion and have access to grace. Jews: the covenant remains. Muslims, with us, adore one God. Those who ‘through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but sincerely seek God and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience—those too may achieve eternal salvation.’ (LG 16)”

Say: “So the answer to ‘Can non-Catholics be saved?’ is yes, through Christ and in some way related to the Church, even if they don’t know it. This is not indifferentism (‘all religions are equal’) nor ‘anonymous Christianity’ as such. The Church rejects any idea that one can reject Christ and the Church knowingly and be saved (LG 14). Also, the Church doesn’t deny the possibility of salvation for non-Christians. Their salvation is by Christ’s grace. Also related: baptism of desire and blood; limbo (a theory not taught as doctrine; the 2007 International Theological Commission document gives grounds for hope for unbaptized infants). Also: Pope Pius IX’s ‘invincible ignorance.’ Francis Xavier’s sorrow over unbaptized persons contrasts with the clearer teaching of Vatican II.”

Say: “What difference does it make? If people can be saved without knowing the Church, why evangelize? The Church’s answer: (1) Christ commanded it; (2) the Gospel is the fullness of truth and a gift that everyone deserves; (3) the Church provides the sacraments, community and clarity; (4) we don’t know the fate of any individual, so we have urgency; (5) evangelization is love: we want others to know the one who loves them. Paul: ‘Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!’ (1 Corinthians 9:16) We hold both: confidence in God’s mercy and urgency of mission. The magi show that God leads people by many ways to Christ, using their own gifts and questions. Be careful to avoid two errors: ‘only Catholics are saved’ and ‘it doesn’t matter what you believe.’ Hope: the Church prays for the salvation of all.”
ask: Can non-Catholics be saved? (Yes, through Christ, if they sincerely seek God and follow conscience through no fault of their own.)
Why evangelize if so? (Christ commanded it; the Gospel is a gift; the Church provides the fullness of the means.)
What two errors should we avoid? (Only Catholics are saved; it doesn’t matter what you believe.)
practice: Make a chart of groups: baptized Catholics, other Christians, Jews, Muslims, those who never heard of Christ, those who reject the Church knowingly.
Write what the Church teaches about each, with Lumen Gentium references.
Write a careful two-sentence statement on salvation for a friend.
List three ways to evangelize without arguing.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you desire all to be saved. Make us instruments of your mercy.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Explain this teaching to someone.”

tryit: Sort Church statements about salvation.
Mark what is certain and what is hope.
Write your own careful statement.
lessons.saintStory:
Matthew’s Gospel tells that after Jesus was born in Bethlehem, magi from the East came to Jerusalem, asking, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to worship him.” They were probably learned men, astronomers or priests of a Persian or Babylonian tradition. They were not Jews. They had no Scripture; they had the sky, and a longing for truth.
King Herod and the chief priests, who knew the Scriptures, told them: Bethlehem. The magi followed the star and found the child with Mary his mother. They knelt and worshiped him, and offered gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home by another way.
The Church celebrates this on Epiphany. The Fathers saw the magi as the first fruits of the Gentiles, a sign that Christ came for all nations. They sought sincerely, and were led by what light they had to the one true Light. Tradition names them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

units.title: The moral life: acts, law and grace
units.eq: How do law and grace work together in a moral life?

lessons.title: The morality of human acts
lessons.idea: An act is good only if its object, intention and circumstances are good. The end does not justify the means. Passions and feelings are part of being human and are meant to be guided by reason.
lessons.question: What makes an act good or bad?
lessons.activity: Analyze cases using the three sources of morality (object, intention, circumstances). Write what changes if each one changes.
teach: The morality of an act depends on the object (what we choose), the intention (why), and the circumstances (CCC 1750–1754). All three must be good (CCC 1755).
A good intention does not make a bad act good; the end does not justify the means (CCC 1753, 1756; Romans 3:8). Some acts are always wrong (intrinsically evil) (CCC 1756).
Passions (love, fear, anger, joy) are not bad in themselves; they become good or evil depending on how reason guides them (CCC 1762–1770). Virtue orders the passions (CCC 1767–1770).
Circumstances can increase or lessen responsibility but cannot make a bad act good (CCC 1754).
talk: Which feelings are hardest to guide?
Can you think of a case where circumstances change responsibility?
quiz: The three sources of morality are…|Rules, fear, habit|Time, place, people|Feelings, plans, luck|Object, intention, circumstances|3|CCC 1750.
The end justifies the means is…|Sometimes right|Wrong|Right|Always right|1|CCC 1759.
Passions are…|Always good|Always bad|Irrelevant|Neither good nor bad in themselves|3|CCC 1767.
lessons.life: Choose one decision this week and examine its object, intention and circumstances.
lessons.saint: Ivo of Kermartin: a judge who defended the poor without a fee.
lessons.mem: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If someone steals to feed their family, is it good, bad or both?” Let students argue before introducing the three sources.
lessons.assess: Ask students to analyze a case with the three sources of morality.

script.open: Read two short cases aloud. In one, a student lies to protect a friend from a bully. In the other, a student lies to avoid a punishment. Ask, “Same act or different?” and write down the words they use to separate them.
teach: Say: “The Catechism (CCC 1749-1761) teaches that the morality of human acts depends on three sources. The object: the act itself, what is chosen, ‘the proximate end of a deliberate decision.’ The intention: ‘the end for which we act,’ which lies in the acting person’s will. The circumstances: the who, what, where, when, how, and the consequences. ‘A morally good act requires the goodness of the object, of the end, and of the circumstances together.’ If the object is evil, the act is evil, regardless of the intention. ‘The end does not justify the means.’ A good intention (e.g., giving to the poor out of vanity) does not make an evil act good, and a bad intention spoils a good act (e.g., giving alms to be praised; Matthew 6:1-4).”

Say: “Intrinsically evil acts: acts which, by their object, are always wrong, regardless of intention or circumstances. Examples: murder of the innocent, adultery, rape, torture, lying, blasphemy, direct abortion, euthanasia. Veritatis Splendor (1993), by John Paul II, defends this against proportionalism and consequentialism, which hold that an act’s morality depends on the proportion of good and bad results. The Church answers: no; a person may never do evil that good may come of it (Romans 3:8). Circumstances can increase or reduce guilt, but they cannot change an act’s species. Reduced responsibility: ignorance, fear, force, habit. Double effect: when an act has both a good and an evil effect, it may be permissible if (1) the act itself is good or neutral, (2) the good effect isn’t obtained by the evil effect, (3) the evil is not intended, and (4) there is a proportionately grave reason.”

Say: “Passions. Emotions aren’t good or bad in themselves; they become morally good or evil as they are governed by reason and will. Virtue directs the passions. A judge like Ivo must weigh facts, law and mercy. Some practical use: when a moral decision is hard, ask three questions. What am I doing, exactly? Why am I doing it? What are the circumstances and likely consequences? Then check with the Church’s teaching. Moral absolutes protect the weak. Pope John Paul II: ‘The Church… does not hold that conscience can create moral truth.’ Ivo’s example: he used his skill for justice and mercy, and refused the temptation to make exceptions for gain. Many modern debates turn on this question: whether results alone decide.”
ask: What are the three sources of morality? (Object, intention, circumstances.)
Can a good intention justify an evil act? (No.)
What is proportionalism? (The theory that morality depends only on the proportion of good and bad results; the Church rejects it.)
practice: Analyze three cases by object, intention and circumstances: a nurse lies to protect a patient from an abuser; a student cheats to keep a scholarship; a doctor prescribes strong pain medication to a dying patient.
Identify the object, the intention and the circumstances of each.
Decide if any act is intrinsically evil.
Apply double effect where relevant.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me clear sight and a just heart.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Analyze a decision you face by the three sources.”

tryit: Analyze three actions by object, intention and circumstances.
Identify an intrinsically evil act.
Explain proportionalism’s error.
lessons.saintStory:
Ivo Hélory of Kermartin was born around 1253 in Brittany, France, into a noble family. He studied law and theology in Paris and Orléans. Returning to Brittany, he was appointed an ecclesiastical judge in Rennes, then in Tréguier. He became known for his fairness and incorruptibility. He refused bribes, listened to every case, and tried to reconcile the parties before judgment. He is said to have often paid the legal costs of poor litigants and represented them for free, earning the title “advocate of the poor.”
He was ordained a priest in 1284 and served as a parish pastor while continuing as a judge. He gave away his income, wore plain clothes and fasted. He visited prisoners and cared for the sick, orphans and beggars. He died in 1303 and was canonized in 1347.
He is the patron of lawyers and judges. There is an old saying in Brittany about him: “Sanctus Yvo erat Brito, advocatus et non latro, res miranda populo” (“St. Ivo was a Breton, a lawyer and not a thief, a thing to marvel at”).

lessons.title: Law: eternal, natural, Old and New
lessons.idea: God’s law is the plan of his wisdom. It is shown in the natural law written on our hearts, in the Old Law (Decalogue), and in the New Law of Christ, which is love and the grace of the Spirit.
lessons.question: How do natural law, Old Law and New Law relate?
lessons.activity: Create a chart with columns: eternal law, natural law, Old Law, New Law, civil law. Fill in definitions, sources, purposes and examples. Discuss how civil laws can be just or unjust.
teach: The eternal law is God’s plan for the universe (CCC 1950). The natural law is the participation of the rational creature in it, “the light of understanding placed in us by God” (CCC 1954–1960).
The Old Law is a preparation for the Gospel; the Decalogue states what reason can know (CCC 1961–1964). The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit, the law of love and freedom (CCC 1965–1974).
Civil laws bind in conscience when they are just; an unjust law does not oblige (CCC 1902, 2242). Conscientious objection is a duty when laws require evil.
Jesus fulfills the law (Matthew 5:17). The Sermon on the Mount is its charter (CCC 1966).
talk: What is the difference between a rule and a law of love?
When might a civil law conflict with natural law?
How does grace change the way we keep the law?
quiz: Natural law is…|A civil law|Moral law known by reason|A feeling|A custom|1|CCC 1954.
The New Law is…|Mere suggestion|The grace of the Holy Spirit and love|Optional|A new set of rules|1|CCC 1966.
An unjust civil law…|Does not bind in conscience|Is divine|Is fine|Always binds|0|CCC 1903.
lessons.life: Read the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) over three days and note one way to live it.
lessons.saint: Raymond of Peñafort: a lawyer who organized the Church’s laws into one book.
misc: “Natural law is only a Catholic idea.”
“The New Law abolishes the Ten Commandments.”
lessons.mem: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free.” (Romans 8:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How do you know some things are wrong even without a rule?” Introduce natural law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the relationship of the four laws.

script.open: Write the word ‘law’ on the board and ask students to list every kind of law they can think of in sixty seconds. Group them into columns: civil, school, family, moral, natural. Keep the board for the lesson.
teach: Say: “Aquinas, in the Summa, defines law as ‘an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated.’ He distinguishes four kinds. Eternal law: God’s wisdom guiding all creation. Natural law: the human participation in the eternal law, known by reason, written on the heart (Romans 2:14-15). It commands to do good and avoid evil, preserve life, seek truth, live in society. It is universal and immutable. Human (positive) law: laws made by legitimate authority, applying natural law to circumstances. Divine law: revealed law, the Old Law and the New Law. The Catechism (1950-1986) presents this.”

Say: “The Old Law: the law of Moses, the Ten Commandments. ‘Holy, just and good’ (Romans 7:12) but imperfect: it points to Christ but cannot give the grace to fulfill it. It is a preparation for the Gospel, a tutor (Galatians 3:24). Its moral precepts remain; ceremonial and civil precepts are fulfilled in Christ. The New Law: the law of the Gospel, ‘the grace of the Holy Spirit received by faith in Christ’ (Aquinas). It is law of love, of grace and of freedom. The Sermon on the Mount, the Beatitudes, the Lord’s Prayer. It does not abolish the Old but fulfills it, adding the counsels (e.g., poverty, chastity, obedience). Its power: the Holy Spirit within.”

Say: “Unjust laws. Aquinas and Augustine: ‘an unjust law is no law at all’ in the sense that it has no binding moral force, though one may sometimes comply to avoid greater harm. Martin Luther King Jr., in his Letter from Birmingham Jail, cited Aquinas: ‘An unjust law is a human law that is not rooted in eternal law and natural law.’ The Church teaches that citizens have a duty of conscience not to follow directives that contradict the moral order (CCC 2242). ‘We must obey God rather than men.’ (Acts 5:29) Conscientious objection. Civil disobedience, with a nonviolent spirit, is sometimes justified. Canon law: the Church’s own law, which is human law ordered to the salvation of souls; ‘the supreme law is the salvation of souls.’ Raymond’s service shows that law at its best serves justice and charity.”
ask: What are the four kinds of law? (Eternal, natural, human, divine.)
What is the New Law? (The grace of the Holy Spirit, the law of love and freedom.)
How should we respond to unjust laws? (Follow conscience, nonviolently, obeying God rather than men.)
practice: Make a chart with five laws: eternal, natural, Old, New, civil. Give an example of each.
Choose one civil law and analyze whether it is just by natural law.
Read a paragraph of King’s Letter from Birmingham Jail.
Write a short paragraph on when disobedience is justified.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, write your law on our hearts.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the Letter from Birmingham Jail.”

tryit: Distinguish eternal, natural, Old, New and civil law.
Give an example of each.
Explain what makes a law unjust.
lessons.saintStory:
Raymond was born around 1175 in Catalonia, Spain. He studied canon and civil law at Bologna and became a professor. In 1222 he joined the Dominicans, and soon after Pope Gregory IX called him to Rome. Gregory asked him to organize the many scattered decrees of popes and councils, which contradicted one another and made it hard for judges and bishops. Raymond spent about three years on this work, and in 1234, the Decretals of Gregory IX was published. It became the main law book of the Church for nearly 700 years, until the Code of Canon Law of 1917.
Raymond also wrote a handbook for confessors, the Summa de casibus poenitentiae, and helped found the Mercedarians, an order that rescued Christian captives. He was elected Master General of the Dominicans in 1238 but resigned after two years because of his health. He is said to have urged missionaries to learn Arabic and Hebrew.
He died in 1275, aged about a hundred. He was canonized in 1601 and is patron of canon lawyers.

lessons.title: Grace, justification and merit
lessons.idea: Grace is God’s free gift that makes us his children. Justification forgives sin and makes us holy. We cooperate with grace, and God rewards what he himself begins in us.
lessons.question: How do grace and effort work together?
lessons.activity: Study the Catholic and Lutheran agreement in the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999). Write a one-page statement on grace and works, with quotes from Scripture and the Catechism.
teach: Justification is God’s gift, removing sin and communicating righteousness through faith and Baptism (CCC 1987–1995). Its source is God’s mercy and Christ’s sacrifice (CCC 1992).

Grace is “the free and undeserved help that God gives us” (CCC 1996). Sanctifying grace makes us holy; actual grace helps us act (CCC 1999–2000). The Spirit works in us “both to will and to work” (Philippians 2:13).
Merit: we cannot earn the first grace, but God’s grace enables us to merit further graces and eternal life (CCC 2006–2011). Holiness is the fullness of Christian life (CCC 2012–2016).
The 1999 Joint Declaration on Justification shows Catholics and Lutherans share a basic consensus.
talk: Why is grace a gift and not a wage?
What does “work out your salvation with fear and trembling” mean?
How should we speak about grace with Protestant friends?
quiz: Grace is…|A reward for deeds|A wage|A feeling|A free and undeserved gift|3|CCC 1996.
Can we earn the first grace?|Never needed|Sometimes|Yes, by good works|No, it is a gift|3|CCC 2010.
The Joint Declaration on Justification was signed in…|2020|1999|1517|1965|1|CCC context.
lessons.life: Thank God for a gift you did not earn and respond with a concrete act of love.
lessons.saint: Caesarius of Arles: a bishop whose council at Orange taught that even the beginning of faith is a gift.
lessons.mem: “For by grace you have been saved through faith.” (Ephesians 2:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Can you earn a gift? What do you do with one?” Use gifts to introduce grace.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain justification, grace and merit in their own words.

script.open: Ask, “If someone gives you a gift, you can accept it or refuse it. If a drowning person is thrown a rope, he can grab it. But who made the rope, threw it and gave strength to grab it? Where does our part start?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Justification is the work of God’s grace that makes us righteous. The Catechism (1987-2029): ‘Justification is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man.’ (Trent) It is the most excellent work of God’s mercy. It comes through faith in Jesus Christ and Baptism. It conforms us to the righteousness of God, who makes us inwardly just. It is God’s initiative: ‘the first work of the grace of the Holy Spirit is conversion.’ We can’t earn it. Paul: ‘For by grace you have been saved through faith… not because of works, lest any man should boast.’ (Ephesians 2:8-9) Yet ‘faith working through love’ (Galatians 5:6). Trent: we cooperate freely with grace, which doesn’t destroy freedom.”

Say: “Errors. Pelagianism (Pelagius, c. 400): humans can achieve salvation by their own efforts; grace is merely help; denies original sin. Condemned; Augustine opposed it. Semi-Pelagianism: we can take the first step; condemned at Orange 529. Reformation views: Luther held that we are justified by faith alone, righteousness is imputed (credited) externally, and good works are fruits but do not contribute. Calvin added predestination. Catholic response at Trent (1547): justification is real interior renewal, by grace; faith is the beginning, but it must be formed by charity; good works are meritorious by grace; one can lose justification through mortal sin and regain it through Penance. The 1999 Joint Declaration with Lutherans found a consensus: ‘By grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit.’”

Say: “Merit. The Church teaches that we can merit eternal life and an increase of grace, but only because of God’s grace and the merits of Christ. ‘When God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts.’ (Augustine) Merit is not a claim on God by justice, but a gift God gives, because he wills to associate us in his work. Thérèse of Lisieux prayed: ‘I wish to be clothed in your own justice and to receive from your love the eternal possession of yourself.’ Perseverance: a gift. Assurance: we hope for salvation but cannot be certain of final perseverance without special revelation; we trust in God’s mercy. Predestination: God wills all to be saved; the Church does not teach that anyone is predestined to hell. Practical: we pray, ‘Lord, I can’t without you’ and also ‘I will cooperate.’ Grace and freedom are not rivals.”
ask: What is justification? (God’s work of making us righteous inwardly, by grace.)
What did the Council of Orange teach? (Even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace.)
What is merit? (God rewards what his grace enables us to do.)
practice: Make a three-column chart: Pelagian / Reformation / Catholic account of justification.
Fill in on what causes our salvation, the role of works and assurance.
Write a plain-language explanation of Catholic teaching for a Protestant friend.
Share and check with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, without you I can do nothing; with you, all things.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Ephesians 2:1-10.”

tryit: Lay out the Catholic account of justification.
Contrast it with Pelagian and Reformation views.
Explain merit.
lessons.saintStory:
Caesarius was born around 470 in Gaul, to a Christian family. As a teenager he joined the monastery on the island of Lérins, but his health failed and he went to Arles. In 502, at about thirty-two, he was made bishop of Arles, a position he held for forty years. He was a pastor, caring for the poor, redeeming captives and building hospitals. He wrote a rule for nuns, one of the first for women in Gaul, which his sister Caesaria followed as abbess.
He preached simple sermons in the vernacular, designed to be understood by ordinary people, and urged them to attend Mass, pray and give alms. In 529, he presided over the Council of Orange, which settled a dispute about grace. Some, called semi-Pelagians, taught that people could take the first step toward God on their own, and that grace followed. The council, with the pope’s approval, taught that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace.
Caesarius died in 542. The decisions of Orange were later used at the Council of Trent.

units.title: The tradition of prayer
units.eq: How does the Church teach us to pray?

lessons.title: The Psalms and Mary at prayer
lessons.idea: The Psalms are the prayer book of Israel and the Church. Mary’s prayer, from the Annunciation to Pentecost, is a model for our prayer: she listens, says yes and prays with the Church.
lessons.question: What do the Psalms and Mary teach about prayer?
lessons.activity: Pray a Psalm in three ways (aloud, sung and silently). Then pray the Magnificat and write your own “magnificat” of thanks.
teach: The Psalms express every human mood and were Jesus’ prayer book (CCC 2585–2589). The Church prays them in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours.
Mary’s prayer: the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), her presence at Cana, at the Cross and at Pentecost (Acts 1:14) (CCC 2617–2619). She prays for us and with us.
The Hail Mary and the Rosary are Marian prayers that lead to Christ (CCC 2676–2678). The Magnificat is evening prayer each day in the Church.
Praying the Psalms with Jesus helps us pray in dark times too (Psalm 88).
talk: Which Psalm speaks to you now?
What does the Magnificat reveal about Mary?
How does the Rosary help you pray?
quiz: The Psalms are…|The Church’s prayer book|A calendar|A history book|A law code|0|CCC 2585.
The Magnificat is…|A psalm of David|Mary’s song of praise|A hymn of Paul|A creed|1|Luke 1:46.
The Rosary leads us to…|Mary only|Saints only|Christ|Silence|2|CCC 2678.
lessons.life: Pray one psalm each day this week and the Magnificat in the evening.
lessons.saint: Pius V: a Dominican pope who asked all Christendom to pray the Rosary before the Battle of Lepanto.
lessons.mem: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.” (Luke 1:46–47)
lessons.hook: Read part of Psalm 22 and Psalm 150. Ask what feelings they show and why the Psalms include both.
lessons.assess: Ask students to pray a psalm and explain what it teaches about prayer.

script.open: Pass around a rosary or a psalter and invite each student to hold it for a few seconds. Say, “Both are prayers someone gave you words for. What is the advantage of praying with someone else’s words?”
teach: Say: “The Psalms are the prayer book of the Church. Jesus prayed them: at the Last Supper they sang the Hallel (Psalms 113-118), and on the cross he prayed Psalm 22. The Church prays them daily in the Liturgy of the Hours and at every Mass. Athanasius said that most of Scripture speaks to us, but the Psalms speak for us: ‘the Psalter has this marvel: it contains all the movements of our souls.’ Types: praise, thanksgiving, trust, lament, repentance, royal psalms (fulfilled in Christ), wisdom. Praying them: read slowly, enter into the situation, hear Christ praying, make it your own. The Church ends each psalm with the Gloria Patri, giving them a Christian sense.”

Say: “Mary at prayer. Luke shows her receptive: ‘Let it be to me according to your word’; the Magnificat, composed of Old Testament echoes (Hannah’s song); she ‘kept all these things, pondering them in her heart’; at Cana she intercedes; at the cross she stands; in the upper room she prays with the apostles. The Catechism (2617-2619) calls her the model of prayer. The Hail Mary: the angel’s greeting, Elizabeth’s greeting, and the Church’s petition. The Rosary: a Gospel in miniature. John Paul II in Rosarium Virginis Mariae (2002): it is ‘a compendium of the Gospel’; ‘to recite the Rosary is nothing other than to contemplate with Mary the face of Christ.’ He added the Luminous Mysteries. How to pray it: begin with the Sign of the Cross and Creed; each decade: announce the mystery, Our Father, ten Hail Marys, Glory Be, and the Fatima prayer; end with the Hail, Holy Queen.”

Say: “Other Marian prayers: the Angelus, Regina Caeli, Memorare, Salve Regina, the Litany of Loreto, the Magnificat, Marian consecration (Montfort). Understand the theology: we pray ‘to’ Mary in the sense of asking her to pray for us: ‘pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death.’ Mary leads to Jesus: ‘Do whatever he tells you.’ The Rosary’s fruits: contemplation, peace, intercession. Pius V and Lepanto: Catholics believed in the power of the Rosary for intercession. Misunderstandings: Rosary as repetition: Jesus warns against babbling (Matthew 6:7), but repetition with attention can quiet the mind, as a mantra of love. A practical start: one decade a day. Use beads, an app or fingers. Don’t worry about distractions.”
ask: Why do we pray the Psalms? (Jesus prayed them; the Church prays them; they cover every feeling.)
What did John Paul II call the Rosary? (A compendium of the Gospel.)
What happened at Lepanto? (The Christian fleet defeated the Ottoman fleet in 1571 after the Rosary was prayed.)
practice: Pray Psalm 23 slowly in the first person, then in the voice of Christ.
Pray one decade of the Rosary together (e.g., the Annunciation), pausing to picture the scene at each Hail Mary.
Write three things Mary teaches about prayer.
Choose a daily rhythm: one psalm and one decade.
script.close: Pray the Hail, Holy Queen. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray a decade daily this week.”

tryit: Pray a psalm in the Church’s way.
Pray a decade of the Rosary with a Gospel scene.
Write what Mary teaches about prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Antonio Ghislieri was born in 1504 in northern Italy, to a poor family. He worked as a shepherd as a boy, then entered the Dominicans at fourteen. He became a strict inquisitor and bishop, a man of prayer and penance. He was elected pope in 1566 as Pius V. He lived simply, still wearing his white Dominican habit, which is why popes dress in white.
He implemented the Council of Trent: he published the Roman Catechism (1566), the Roman Breviary (1568), and the Roman Missal (1570), which standardized the Mass for centuries. In 1571, the Ottoman Turkish fleet threatened Europe. Pius organized the Holy League of Spain, Venice and the papal states, and asked Catholics to pray the Rosary. On October 7, 1571, the Christian fleet won an unexpected victory at the Battle of Lepanto. Pius reportedly knew of it before the news arrived. He attributed the victory to Our Lady and instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now Our Lady of the Rosary, on October 7.
He died in 1572 and was canonized in 1712.

lessons.title: Guides in prayer: saints and spiritual traditions
lessons.idea: The Church has many schools of prayer taught by saints: Benedictine, Franciscan, Ignatian, Carmelite, Salesian and others. They show that there are many ways to pray and the same Spirit teaches all.
lessons.question: Which school of prayer fits me?
lessons.activity: Sample short practices from three traditions: Benedictine lectio, Ignatian imagination, Carmelite silence. Reflect on which fits, and plan to try one for two weeks.
teach: The saints are guides in prayer (CCC 2683–2684). Each spiritual family has a charism: Benedictine (liturgy and lectio), Franciscan (simplicity, creation), Dominican (study and preaching), Carmelite (contemplation), Ignatian (discernment and finding God in all things), Salesian (devout life for all).
Other guides: the family, pastors, religious communities, catechesis and spiritual direction (CCC 2685–2690). Places and times of prayer support it (CCC 2691–2696).
All schools lead to Christ in the Church (CCC 2684). No method replaces relationship.
Encourage students to ask a trusted guide before taking on intense practices.
talk: Who has taught you to pray?
What practice would you like to try?
Why do we need a guide?
quiz: Ignatian spirituality stresses…|Discernment and finding God in all things|Chant only|Silence only|Work only|0|CCC 2684 context.
A spiritual director is…|A teacher of math|A guide in prayer and life|A judge|A confessor only|1|CCC 2690.
All schools of prayer lead to…|Fame|Christ|A method|Silence|1|CCC 2684.
lessons.life: Try one new practice for two weeks and note what you learn, then talk to a mentor.
lessons.saint: Seraphim of Sarov: a Russian monk whose greeting to every visitor was, “My joy, Christ is risen!”
misc: “There is only one correct way to pray.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Ask students to describe how a favorite athlete or musician practices. Say that saints are coaches in prayer.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe two schools of prayer and choose a practice.

script.open: Spread out the covers of four spiritual classics, such as Confessions, Introduction to the Devout Life, The Interior Castle and Story of a Soul. Ask students to pick the one they would open first, and say why.
teach: Say: “The Church has many schools of spirituality, each a way of following Christ, shaped by a saint. They don’t compete but complement. Benedictine: ‘Ora et labora.’ Liturgical prayer, the Rule, stability, hospitality, lectio divina. Franciscan: poverty, joy, love of creation, the humanity of Christ (the crèche, the cross). Dominican: study, preaching, truth, the Rosary. Carmelite: contemplative prayer, the interior life (Teresa, John of the Cross, Thérèse). Ignatian: finding God in all things, discernment, the Examen, the Spiritual Exercises, ‘for the greater glory of God.’ Salesian (Francis de Sales): holiness for all, gentleness, devotion in ordinary life. Vincentian: service of the poor. Marian (Montfort): consecration to Jesus through Mary. Eastern: the Jesus Prayer, icons, hesychasm, theosis (Seraphim).”

Say: “Modern movements: Opus Dei (sanctify work), Focolare (unity), Communion and Liberation, Neocatechumenal Way, Schoenstatt, Taizé (simple chant, silence), Charismatic Renewal, Catholic Worker (Dorothy Day: service and peace), Sant’Egidio, L’Arche (living with people with disabilities), the Little Way of Thérèse. Each has a charism: a gift of the Spirit for the Church. How do we choose? We don’t have to choose just one. The question is: which helps me to know, love and follow Christ? Practical: read the biography of a saint; try their method; ask a spiritual director; join a group. Spiritual direction: a regular conversation with a wise person to help discern God’s work in your life.”

Say: “Spiritual reading and life. Read the saints: Confessions (Augustine), Story of a Soul (Thérèse), The Interior Castle (Teresa), Introduction to the Devout Life (Francis de Sales), Imitation of Christ, The Way of a Pilgrim (Eastern), Abandonment to Divine Providence (de Caussade), Divine Mercy in My Soul (Faustina). Guard against distortions: consumer spirituality, emotionalism, individualism. The test: it leads to humility, love of Christ, the Church and neighbor. Seraphim: his peace and joy flowed from the Jesus Prayer and years of silence. His example prompts us to find a deeper interior life. ‘Acquire the spirit of peace and thousands around you will be saved.’ Peace is mission.”
ask: Name two schools of spirituality and their emphasis. (Ignatian: finding God in all things; Carmelite: contemplation.)
What is spiritual direction? (Regular guidance to discern God’s work in your life.)
What is the test of a spirituality? (Whether it leads to humility, love of Christ, the Church and neighbor.)
practice: Make a table of five schools: founder, emphasis, practice, one book.
Choose one practice to try for a month (Examen, lectio, Jesus Prayer, the Little Way, Rosary).
Plan when and how you will do it.
Choose a book to read.
script.close: Pray the Jesus Prayer together slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Greet someone today with joy, as Seraphim did.”

tryit: Compare three schools of spirituality.
Choose one to try for a month.
Write what it adds to your prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Seraphim of Sarov was born Prokhor Moshnin in 1754 in Kursk, Russia, to a merchant family. As a boy he fell from a bell tower and was said to be miraculously unhurt; he fell gravely ill, and had a vision of Mary, who healed him. At nineteen he entered the monastery of Sarov. He became a hermit in a cabin in the forest. For a thousand days and nights he knelt on a rock, praying the Jesus Prayer with his hands raised. In 1804, robbers beat him nearly to death, leaving him with a stoop, and he forgave them.
After years of silence, he began to receive visitors, in obedience to a vision. Thousands came for advice. He greeted everyone, rich or poor, with a bow and the Easter greeting, “My joy, Christ is risen!” and called them “my joy.” He fed the bears in the forest from his hand.
He taught: “Acquire the spirit of peace, and thousands around you will be saved.” He died in 1833, kneeling in front of an icon. He is among the most beloved Russian Orthodox saints; Catholics also honor the holiness of the Eastern saints.

lessons.title: Obstacles to prayer and persevering
lessons.idea: Prayer is a battle against distraction, dryness, discouragement and acedia. Jesus gave parables of persistence, and the Church teaches humility, trust and perseverance. The Our Father is the school of prayer.
lessons.question: What helps when prayer is hard?
lessons.activity: Make a personal “when prayer is hard” card with five practical steps (return, simplify, sit with a psalm, ask a friend to pray, go to the sacraments). Share one with a partner.
teach: The battle of prayer includes distraction, dryness, presumption and acedia (CCC 2725–2733). A distraction is not a failure; return gently (CCC 2729).
Discouragement and doubt about whether God hears can be answered by humility, trust and persistence (CCC 2734–2741). Jesus says, “Ask, and it will be given you” (Luke 11:9).
Pray without ceasing means making prayer a habit, supported by liturgy and short prayers (CCC 2742–2745). The Our Father is the model.
Seek help if dryness comes with deeper sadness; spiritual direction and counseling both help.
talk: What is your biggest obstacle in prayer?
How do you return after distraction?
Why does Jesus tell us to persist?
quiz: A good response to distraction is…|Gently return to God|Quit|Skip prayer|Get upset|0|CCC 2729.
Acedia is…|Spiritual laziness or discouragement|A feast|A rule|A prayer|0|CCC 2733.
The widow in Luke 18 teaches…|Anger|Persistence|Silence|Fear|1|Luke 18:1.
lessons.life: Choose a fixed time and place to pray for two weeks, and when you wander, return gently.
lessons.saint: Jane de Chantal: a widow and foundress who prayed through forty years of darkness.
misc: “God doesn’t answer unless I feel something.”
lessons.mem: “Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
lessons.hook: Read the story of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8). Ask: “Why does Jesus tell us this?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three obstacles and a remedy for each.

script.open: Ask, “When you pray, what gets in the way? Tiredness, boredom, doubt, distraction, busyness, feeling nothing? Which is yours?” Take honest answers. List them.
teach: Say: “The Catechism (2725-2745) lists obstacles to prayer and ways to meet them. Distractions: the commonest. Remedy: return gently to God; offer them; don’t fight. Dryness: a feeling that God is absent; may be a test or purification. Remedy: persevere in fidelity; ‘prayer is a battle’ (CCC 2725). Acedia (spiritual sloth): ‘a form of depression due to lax ascetical practice, decreasing vigilance, carelessness of heart.’ Remedy: determination. Discouragement: failure to pray, thinking you’re no good at it. Remedy: humility; God is patient. Busyness: no time. Remedy: schedule it; prayer is not an extra. Doubt: ‘Is anyone listening?’ Remedy: faith; ask for faith; the Psalms are honest. Unanswered prayer: ‘We do not know how to pray as we ought.’ (Romans 8:26) Trust the Spirit.”

Say: “Perseverance. Jesus taught persistence: the widow and the unjust judge (Luke 18:1-8), the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5-13). ‘Pray at all times and do not lose heart.’ The dark night: John of the Cross taught that God sometimes withdraws consolations to purify love. Mother Teresa lived for decades without a sense of God’s presence, and kept serving. Jane de Chantal’s forty years of dryness. Even Jesus on the cross: ‘My God, why have you forsaken me?’ Faith is not a feeling. The measure of prayer is love, not consolation. Practical helps: a regular time and place; a simple method; a prayer partner; spiritual direction; the sacraments; the Psalms; Scripture; silence; reading the saints; short prayers during the day; fasting; being generous. Prayer is a gift to ask for.”

Say: “A last reflection. Prayer will continue after the course ends. Make a plan for dry times: What will I do when I don’t feel like praying? Whom will I tell? What will I do for just five minutes? Francis de Sales advised Jane: ‘Do not be disturbed; simply remain faithful.’ And ‘Have patience with all things, but first of all with yourself.’ Prayer is a relationship with a loving Father. Like any relationship, it has seasons. The fruit: peace, love, service. Pray the Our Father with attention. God is faithful. ‘Be still, and know that I am God.’ (Psalm 46:10) Your course ends here, but your life of prayer is just beginning. ‘The Lord bless you and keep you.’”
ask: What is acedia? (Spiritual sloth; carelessness of heart in prayer.)
How should we handle distractions? (Return gently to God.)
What did Jane de Chantal do during her forty years of dryness? (She persevered in fidelity.)
practice: Make two columns: obstacles to my prayer / remedies.
Add a plan for the next dry season: what I will do, whom I will tell, what is the minimum five-minute prayer.
Write a short prayer to say when you feel nothing.
Share your plan with a partner and commit to check in monthly.
script.close: Pray the Priestly Blessing: “The Lord bless you and keep you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Keep your prayer plan, especially when you don’t feel like it.”

tryit: List your obstacles to prayer.
Pair each with a remedy.
Make a plan for the next dry season.
lessons.saintStory:
Jane Frances Frémyot was born in 1572 in Dijon, France. She married Baron Christophe de Chantal and had six children, four of whom survived. She ran their estate with skill and generosity. In 1601, her husband was killed in a hunting accident. Jane, at twenty-eight, was devastated. She forgave the man who accidentally shot him, and agreed to be godmother to his child.
In 1604, she met Francis de Sales, bishop of Geneva, who became her spiritual director. Over six years, they developed a plan for a new community for women, the Visitation, who would be able to enter with weaker health or older age than the severe orders. She provided for her children and in 1610 founded the Visitation at Annecy. It grew to eighty houses in her lifetime.
For almost forty years, Jane experienced great inner darkness: dryness, doubts and a sense of God’s absence, even as she led her sisters. Francis’s letters guided her. She persevered with simple fidelity, praying even when she felt nothing. She died in 1641 and was canonized in 1767.
